The Prayer of the Poor of God in the Bible

Fr. Anselmo Dalbesio, OFM Cap.

Biblical refresher course given by Fr. Dalbesio at the Generalate of the Daughters of St. Anne — Rome, June 1991 — and already published in Virga Jesse.

In our reflections on the theme set before us, I shall follow a line of development that obeys a precise logical criterion.

First of all we shall see who these “Poor of God” are, trying to grasp their identity and their spirituality with a view to understanding their prayer; then we shall examine in depth the characteristics of the prayer of these “poor of God”. We shall then move on to the NT, for reasons that will be stated. After that we shall dwell on the luminous figure of Jesus and, of course, as the faithful mirror of Christ, on that of Mary, so as to see their prayer reflected in two prayers that we pray daily, significantly and not by chance: the Our Father, three times a day (Lauds, Eucharist, Vespers) and the Magnificat, every evening in the celebration of Vespers. The Our Father is par excellence the prayer of Jesus, the Magnificat is the typical prayer of Mary. And they are so not in the sense that they were the formula of prayer verbally used by them, but rather inasmuch as they constitute the perfect X-ray of their praying soul.

This will be, in broad outline, the course we shall follow. Let us begin at once with the underlying theme: “the prayer of the poor” in the Bible. It is evidently not a question of the poor in the absolute, but of the “poor of God”, because poverty as such God does not want; it is not a value. Jesus came to preach evangelical radicalism, which is something quite different from simple material poverty. Here, then, is the meaning that the prayer of the “poor of God” will take on. The qualification “of God” is extremely important, because it is essential and fundamental for the purposes of our discussion.

Let us make two clarifications at once. First of all, the word “poor” is not taken in a merely or predominantly sociological sense, because in the Bible it is always and only used in function of the religious message that is to be conveyed. That is, these are poor people in the real sense, truly poor, not fictitious poor; yet they are considered not for their economic poverty, but for the orientation of their soul, for their religiousness, for what poverty has taught them about the wisdom of life.

Second clarification: we are therefore dealing with poor “of God”, more precisely, with the poor of God of the OT, who are for us the starting point of our discussion, inasmuch as they constitute the historical roots of the purest Christianity, lived in a deep qualitative sense first by Jesus and then by Mary, although in the chronological sense first by Mary and then by Jesus. We shall therefore start from the spirituality of the “Poor of God” of the OT, but in order to move as soon as possible to the Christian newness as it is reflected above all in Mary and in Jesus.

Introduction

In the Bible the poor person is not considered in a sociological sense. This perspective, moreover, would not have made much sense, because Israel was in fact a people whose history always had as its common denominator a constant phenomenon of pauperism. Poverty was therefore not a phenomenon specific to certain individuals, but common to the mass of the nation. Israel was always poor. Hence the evocative value of the image of the banquet, with its abundance of bread and wine and succulent foods (Isaiah), to indicate the messianic times, the times of final salvation with its fullness of life.

Not that a strong message of a social character is absent from the Bible of the OT; think, for example, of Amos, the prophet of social justice, who rails against those who sell their neighbor for a pair of sandals; and this is not a rhetorical figure, a metaphor, but reflects the crude reality of the time. I only mean that the Bible, in this field too, when it speaks of the poor, gives essentially a religious message. Let us then see at once the starting point of this religious discourse on poverty and some self-portraits of these poor of God reflected in the Bible.

1. The Poor of God: Their Religious History and Their Message

The first to identify the future people of God of the last times, that is, the true people of God, with a people of the poor is Zeph 3:11-13. The historical moment of this text, which refers to the future, takes us to the years 640-630 B.C., therefore before the great Babylonian exile:

“On that day you shall no longer be ashamed
of all the deeds by which you rebelled against me;
for then I will remove from your midst
all your proudly exultant ones,
and you shall no longer be haughty
on my holy mountain.
I will leave in the midst of you
a people humble and lowly;
they shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord,
the remnant of Israel.
They shall do no wrong
and utter no lies;
nor shall a deceitful tongue
be found in their mouths.
They shall pasture and lie down,
and none shall make them afraid.”

In this text the term “poor” indicates a person who is physically bent over, because he is afflicted, of lowly spirit because he is wretched, afflicted and bowed down by his own social situation, which has taught him the secret of life and therefore made him meek, devout. This term therefore qualifies the poor man in his fundamental attitude of soul, the one that specifies him on the religious level, and that is condensed in his sense of radical belonging to God. The true poor man, of whom we are speaking, is the one who accepts his situation not out of fatalism, but because he has understood, through the experiences of life, that the things down here are of very little account, that they count for very little, that they are passing, and so he has learned to stake everything on God alone. This type of poor man is thus one who undergoes an experience of great interior liberation. He is a man who has a profound sense of belonging and of radical adherence to God, so that he is indeed “bent, bowed down”, but not in the sense that he passively endures his situation, rather in the sense that he is bowed down before God, recognizes himself as dependent on Him, accepts his belonging to and dependence on the Lord, and thus becomes a synonym for the religious man.

In 712 B.C. there was a first deportation of Israel. When we speak of the exile, we generally think of the Babylonian one of 558 B.C., but Assyria in 712 had already occupied the North, present-day Samaria, and so Israel had been decimated, and only the Kingdom of Judah, comprising the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, had remained intact. The Prophet Zephaniah, starting from this socio-political situation, tells his people that one must become poor before God as one is poor before Assyria, before the great international power of the time. He says: Look, we feel poor before Assyria, which dominates us and uses us at its pleasure, but above all we must know how to become poor before God as we are poor before this foreign power. Material poverty must therefore lead to spiritual poverty, made of authentic faith. Poverty, humanly and historically, even if it is a negative fact, has meaning in a person’s life if it leads to spiritual poverty, if it leads to living and discovering the authenticity of one’s own faith. An authentic faith that takes on shades of abandonment, humility and absolute trust. The faith of the poor man, in this sense, will be a faith that is colored, kneaded with trust, abandonment and confidence. Here is Zeph 2:3 once more:

“Seek the Lord,
all you humble of the earth,
who do his commands;
seek righteousness,
seek humility;
perhaps you may be hidden
on the day of the Lord’s wrath.”

Therefore for Zephaniah the poor man is the one who practices the decrees and the will of God, who surrenders to Him, who accepts Him. Seek righteousness, seek humility, seek this lowly spirit, this spirit surrendered before God, perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In Zeph 3:11-13 we have poverty not set against wealth, but poverty set against pride:

“On that day you shall not be ashamed
of all the deeds by which you rebelled against me;
for then I will remove from your midst
all your proudly exultant ones...”

Therefore the future people of God, the definitive, the true one, will be composed of poor elements, because humble ones, not of poor in a purely social sense, but of the humble and therefore of the poor as set against the proud. This authentic spiritual attitude will bring with it an overall uprightness in moral life. All this, however, in the climate of the Covenant and therefore in the religious perspective. Note: “They shall do no wrong and utter no lies, nor shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouths. They shall pasture and lie down, and none shall make them afraid.”

A century later the Israel of the South too, the Kingdom of Judah, will be deported to Babylon in a violent, tragic way. Then it is all of Israel that collapses. God, however, had made promises to David and these will remain forever: this is the message of Ps 88, which we still pray today in the Liturgy of the Hours at the Office of Readings. The exile in Babylon represented the shattering of all of Israel’s religious certainties wherever they were mistaken, wherever they had been mythologized and read in an excessively human perspective. The exile showed that God is above our history and does not let himself be overcome by our religious ideologies. And Israel, completely stripped, begins to understand. It is in the exile that it experiences the most absolute poverty, because besides material poverty it also experiences spiritual poverty: it has lost the temple, it has lost worship, it has lost the monarchy, it has only the prophets, who administer the word, which moreover is also very fragile, though very alive. But Israel understands, returns to itself and redeems itself, so that from the ashes of the exile the true Israel rises again. The scanty group of those who returned, back in Palestine, had to reckon with those who in the meantime had settled in their place, and so the return to the homeland was an experience as disappointing as the exile. Both experiences are attested by the Psalter; it should be recalled in this regard that the majority of the Psalms date from after the exile. It is in fact the book of songs of the so-called second temple, that is, of the temple that would be built after the exile. For this reason it is above all on the Psalter that we shall dwell in order to examine the prayer of the poor of God.

2. Self-Portrait of the “Poor of God”

The Psalter is the expression of the religiousness of these “poor of God”, precisely because for the most part it comes from the time of the exile and the post-exilic period. The famous Psalm Miserere (Ps 50), for example, reflects a theology, a sensibility and a language typical of the time of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and above all the spiritual world of Jeremiah. But let us start from Ps 149, which we pray at Lauds on the 1st Sunday, above all from its beginning:

“Sing to the Lord a new song,
his praise in the assembly of the faithful...
For the Lord takes delight in his people,
he crowns the humble with victory.”

Note the parallelism: “God takes delight in his people” - “he crowns the humble with victory”. These are humble ones in the sense of poor, of that lowly people who now trust only in God and accept their own situation in a liberating and liberated way. Now this group of the poor is identified in the Psalm simply with the “people of God”. It is they, therefore, who will henceforth constitute the authentic people of the Lord.

Their soul emerges especially from certain Psalms (cf. Ps 9; 10; 25; 34; 37) and above all from Ps 69:30-33: “I am lowly and in pain; let your salvation, O God, protect me” (v. 30). “Let the humble see it and be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive...” (v. 33). The poor man is the one who seeks God, who wears himself out waiting for his Lord, in turning toward Him, in longing for Him. “I am weary with crying out; my throat is parched; my eyes grow dim with waiting for my God” (v. 4). What does it mean, “My eyes grow dim with waiting for my God”? Let us imagine someone who is always gazing at a fixed point in the distance and who thus wears out his sight staring at the horizon, waiting for the Lord to arrive. This sense of waiting for God, this tension toward God, constitutes the north of the magnetic needle of one’s own existence. God then becomes, in a deeply felt way, the foundation, the center of one’s life, because one has acquired the sense of the totality of God, of the all of God.

In this situation the psalmist feels free because he has been liberated within, he feels like an open book before God, he no longer hides from Him. “O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you” (Ps 69:6). Here is the religious poor man of whom we are speaking. Precisely because he has had this experience of liberation from himself, the difficulties of life have taught him not to make himself the absolute point of reference, the center and the epicenter of existence, so that he is a man who has nothing to hide before God and does not want to hide anything; he is a man who no longer plays hide-and-seek with God.

Verse 8 gives another self-portrait of this poor man who risks everything for love of God, that is, who recognizes the primacy of God and lives it: “For your sake I have borne reproach, shame has covered my face”. He is derided because he believes in God, he risks everything for love of God. In v. 10 he feels God’s cause as his own, he is a man now absorbed and as if sucked in by God, he trusts in the Lord alone: “For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult you have fallen on me”. He trusts and stakes everything on God alone and therefore feels himself his servant; God alone can redeem him: “But I pray to You, O Lord, at an acceptable time; in the abundance of your steadfast love, answer me, in the truth of your salvation, O God” (v. 14). One has faith when we feel that God is everything, not merely that He is great or very great; this vision, in fact, is already to set a limit, it is already idolatry. The poor man, then, rejoices in the Lord, seeks Him, and God is for him like his very vital atmosphere. “Let the humble see it and be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive” (v. 33). The joy of life is in proportion to the seeking of God, and a life is serene and joyful to the extent of the charge of seeking God that it possesses. Then life is beautiful and one feels like saying that one would like to be born again a hundred times, a thousand times.

The poor man rejoices in the Lord, seeks Him. These poor are the descendants of the servants of God, they are a link in a long chain. It is the humble set against the proud; thus we have the soul of the two categories, which springs in turn from the two respective existential situations. Whoever is rich, whoever in life has always had everything and has never had to depend on anyone, has never suffered constraints, such a person will never be able to have a sense of attention to others, will inevitably be arrogant, will be proud. Therefore in the Bible having the identity of the poor is not so much the fact of being materially poor, but the fact that this existential situation of life has led him not to rebel against life, as so often happens in the face of suffering and negative things. This existential situation has led him rather to mature a great wisdom of life, to acquire that heart full of wisdom of which the Psalms also speak: “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a wise heart” (Ps 90:12). Therefore the poor man in this sense becomes, as an effect of his situation, humble, modest, gentle, yielding, but not because he has a spineless soul, but because he has acquired true wisdom, has discovered God in the poverty of things, has attained the richness of possessing God; whereas the rich man, by his very situation, is led to become arrogant, haughty, because he has never had the experience of someone who stood before him to make him feel his limits.

Therefore the poor man who turns out well in this sense becomes honest, respects others, because he has learned from life, while the rich man becomes ungodly, because he makes himself a law unto himself. And this can concern our own little religious world too, our personal world, when we want to absolutize our own things and try to maneuver and manage our vital spaces, so that we too become arrogant and ungodly...

Introduction

We have considered the poor of God in their identity and spirituality according to their constant typical character, which is valid in every age. We now wish to dwell on the effects that this spiritual identity had on their prayer, in order to try to grasp the components that must constitute us too as poor of God, and color our prayer, affect it, in a certain way knead it. We could say: “Tell me how you pray and I will tell you who you are”; the “how you are” must be taken, however, not in a formalistic, ritualistic sense, but in a deep, qualitative sense: tell me what your prayer is and I will tell you who you are.

In the Psalms of individual lament we meet a person who complains about his own situation. One would say, at first sight, that a religiosity turned in on itself emerges, and yet the Psalmist, as a member of the people of God, is always under the primordial influence of the experience of God that Israel had at Sinai. This phenomenon occurs in the life of every person and in the life of every human group. The first experience, which we may call primordial, is the one that subsequently structures the psychology of the person, his way of seeing and feeling things.

Every Institute bears the imprint of its founder. You, Daughters of St. Anne, live in a certain way, you express your Christianity according to a certain cut: this derives from the particular Christian experience of your Foundress.

The same holds for Israel’s experience at Sinai; it became not only normative at the ideological level, but structured all of Israel’s subsequent religious experience: the experience of a dialogical God, a God who speaks, who enters into communion, who chooses a people, who becomes a traveling companion in life. Not a fearsome God who punishes, dominates, oppresses, as generally happens in the pagan religions. This concept is expressed in a material way, and so certain great experiences of the Psalter are described with the constants or with the material phenomena that occurred at Sinai. There God manifested himself in thunder, in lightning, that is, through a meteorological phenomenon in which Israel perceived the presence of God. Let us take Ps 17: it is a king who prays, not necessarily David in the historical sense. It begins in a most beautiful way:

“I love you, O Lord, my strength,
O Lord, my rock,
my fortress, my deliverer,
my God, my crag in which I take refuge.”

Here we have five appellations to say God the protector, God who takes charge of our life with all that it contains of risks and dangers. Then he goes on to sing this intervention of God the savior in the life of the psalmist:

“I call upon the Lord, who is worthy to be praised,
and I am saved from my enemies.
The cords of death encompassed me,
the torrents of perdition assailed me.”

1. Adoration and Gratitude

To remember Sinai is not only to remember the experience had there, but to remember the God of the Covenant, the God of Sinai. This is why the most widespread literary form of the Psalter is always the hymn; the Psalms are hymns, that is, songs of thanksgiving and praise. The two great attributes of God in the OT are: the “living” God par excellence, by whom one swears, and the “faithful” God. The Israelite never doubts God’s faithfulness; if anything, he accuses his own unfaithfulness. Let us briefly consider adoration and gratitude; then we shall see the Psalms as the expression of the soul of the “faithful”. Adoration and gratitude are the two greatest expressions of psalmic prayer. In this sense, for us the Psalter is a great teacher of prayer.

a) Adoration

Adoration is condensed in admiration for the greatness of God. We admire him little, because we are not sufficiently in love with God, as is fitting. Gratitude is condensed in the thankful recognition of what God does for his creature. Adoration and gratitude are carried out through the glorifying contemplation of God, of Sacred History, of the faithfulness of the Lord. I said “glorifying contemplation”: one glorifies God because one contemplates him, and when one contemplates God one cannot fail to glorify him, one cannot remain indifferent before his action; and one does not contemplate him in a static way as in a slide, because God is never inert, God is life, he is always in motion according to the testimony of the Bible. All of history, in fact, is a song and a testimony of the faithful God, even when it seems hard to read this faithfulness of God.

Adoration is expressed above all through the liturgical character of Israel’s piety. Liturgical means communal and therefore connotes the praying and adoring action of the community as such. The Israelite never prays as an individual, isolated I, but always as an I who is and feels himself a member of the people of God. Adoration finds its greatest and most genuine expression precisely in public worship, which nourishes and in turn totalizes individual piety. There is no split between collective piety and individual piety; this separation is absurd in the perspective of biblical prayer. We speak of the one and the other separately, but the reality is single. Communal prayer nourishes and gives tone to individual prayer, and individual prayer in turn gives life to communal prayer.

The communal, liturgical prayer of Israel had its principal manifestations, like our Christian liturgy, in the annual feasts: Passover, Pentecost, the feast of Tabernacles, etc., as well as in the daily sacrifices offered in the temple. The psalms of thanksgiving were born for the liturgy in the temple, during which the reading of the Law was celebrated. The liturgy of the word therefore took place in a liturgical climate and reality, that is, of communal prayer. But the liturgy, we know, is not a simple commemoration of the past. In the liturgy of Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles they did not merely commemorate past events, all of which went back to the Exodus, but these were felt as a kind of first pledge of the fulfillment of the promises to the Patriarchs, through the liturgical actualization of all past history, as a saving act and word of God.

The proclamation in the Community of the history of salvation makes sense if there is faith in the people who celebrate it. The proclamation is born of this faith and leads to a further faith, because it is projected into the expectation of the future Messiah, of the Christ. Faith as the environment of liturgical prayer, as its agent, makes us perceive the past events as true in the liturgy being celebrated; as real, because it makes us realize that we are today as we are and here thanks to those past events; we are, as it were, the result of a past also on a human, material, historical level; we are now what we are because we come from that given family, because we have had those given experiences, and therefore the events of the past have forged us, even though we were not physically and historically present. Therefore the past event does not concern only the direct recipients of that time. When we celebrate Easter we do not commemorate only what happened in the last days of Christ’s earthly life outside Jerusalem, in the place called Calvary, with John, Mary and the pious women present, but we bear witness to the conviction of faith that we too were there, because in those past events God had in view all the descendants of humanity, ourselves included. The book of Deuteronomy dates from about 700 B.C., therefore well after the entry into the land of Palestine. And here is how the author speaks in Deut 5:2-3, putting these discourses in the mouth of Moses: “The Lord our God made a covenant with us”. He says “with us” not “with our fathers”, but with us who are alive today, to say that the Covenant of Horeb concerns us, touches us directly, reaches us and addresses us in the first person. It is the Semitic way of speaking by contrast, by antithesis. Not only did God make the covenant with them, but also with us. Hence in the Psalms the accentuated repetition of today: “O that today you would listen to his voice!...” (Ps 95:8). It is God’s today, which then returns in the Letter to the Hebrews, because God speaks continually to each one of us, God is Word, because he is in continual dialogue with us, in communion with each one who comes to the light of this world.

It is in this perspective that the historical Psalms, which are moreover most beautiful (Ps 78, 105, 106, 114), are to be seen. They do not have merely a didactic function, that of recalling the past as history, the teacher of life. The historical Psalms resemble, rather, a catechism that is prayed, meditated, sung. The Psalms celebrate the principal themes of our history of salvation: the Promise, the Exodus, the Covenant, the faithfulness of God. Let us take merely as an example the beautiful Psalm 136, which sings the great moments of Israel’s history in a religious perspective. Each half-verse ends with the expression: his mercy endures forever. God has manifested his mercy, which in Hebrew means “tenderness”, tender love, involved love, which is also mercy. Now what is the meaning of the events? They are seen as the deeds of God, as his great works, the feats, the wonders that the Lord has accomplished in the history of his people, both at the individual and at the communal level. God’s interventions in this history are perceived as great, because where God intervenes everything is great, inasmuch as his action touches life, and life is no small thing. The religious events of the past are therefore a historical testimony to God’s faithfulness.

Ps 105:8 sings: “He is mindful of his covenant forever, of the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations”. God always remembers, he never forgets his covenant. And in the Semitic world and mentality “to remember” means “to do, to carry out” what one does not forget. God always carries out his covenant, on his part he keeps it perennially.

History is, moreover, a testimony of his love. Ps 78:68 states: “He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves”; “to elect” means “to choose”, and if one chooses, one takes in a preferential way; to choose is already an act of love. And then the testimony of his eternal mercy (Ps 136) holds not only for the people of Israel, but for every people, and holds not only for the Community, but also for the individual. Everything that has happened in life is a testimony to the mercy of God. And then the difficulties of prayer disappear; we no longer need so many books to pray when we use the book of our own life as a book of prayer. Then the events, seen in their religious significance with these four valences, strengthen the believing people and therefore also the individual who is a member of it. Then there flowers from our heart first of all thanksgiving joined to repentance; thanking God for his goodness and generosity brings with it repentance and the plea for forgiveness for our unfaithfulness, because we are always inferior to God’s gift, and over the yes to God’s gift there always prevails the no of non-correspondence and inability to accept. Psalms 105 and 106 come to mind in this regard, which express the plea for forgiveness in the refrain.

Moreover, events seen in this light also nourish the demand for a precise practical conduct. If God behaves this way with us, we cannot behave with impunity as we please. In this regard we should recall Ps 78: “Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old, things that we have heard and known, that our ancestors have told us. We will not hide them from their children; we will tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the Lord, and his might, and the wonders that he has done.” Then we recover the value of history-as-teaching with all its pedagogical force directed to inculcating a practical behavior toward God. If God has acted this way with us, we too must behave toward him in a fitting manner. In this perspective, what is the religious sense of history and the sense of this prayer of history? History prayed in this way becomes a true spiritual adventure of universal scope, because in it there is all our personal history.

b) Gratitude

The second component of this psalmic prayer, besides adoration, is gratitude, which is particularly reflected in the awareness of being the “chosen people”. We belong to the people of God. We have seen that the predominant character of Hebrew piety derives from the Covenant, felt as the primordial event that brings Israel to birth as the people of God. It is precisely this datum that gives rise to the vivid awareness of the distinctive biblical face of God. The God of the Bible is a God who lives with us and for us. With Jesus there is a qualitative leap: with him it is no longer merely a matter of the “God with us” of the OT; he is the God with us “who became one of us”. In the OT the awareness of a God who walks with man, who takes charge of our whole human life, is clearly reflected.

In the Psalms there is a strong communal sense of the chosen people, attested by the frequent passage from you to we, as well as by the easy use of the collective I/you: “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want” (Ps 23:1). In this Psalm, as in so many others, the subject who speaks is a collective, communal I, not individualistic or selfish; it is the I of the community. We have seen the prayer of the poor, of these men not turned in on themselves, because they have been inwardly freed from their own ego, people free from the slavery of their own selfishness and their own egocentrism and therefore capable of a prayer thrown upon God, open to Him in the climate of adoration and thanksgiving. Adoration of God and thanksgiving to God, to that God as he historically is, dynamic, communicative, communional, and therefore a prayer that not only prays in life, but that prays one’s own life. It prays one’s own events and thus uses living liturgical books, alive and vital, not printed on dead paper.

2. The Psalms: Expression of the Soul of the Poor Man

In this perspective the Psalms are the expression of the soul of the poor man of God. They are the lived reflection of the poor man of God, of his poverty in the spiritual sense, of one who has acquired an authentic soul before God, of one whom poverty has taught, has made him understand the mystery of life, because life, biblically, before being a problem, is a mystery, which means that when we make it a problem we have already desacralized it, we have already lost its deep meaning. And this prayer of the poor of God in the Psalms is expressed through a host of voices: the sick, prisoners, exiles, the discouraged, those tempted in their faith, sinners. All these various situations, profoundly human and profoundly negative, have created a consciousness, an interior attitude, that of so-called spiritual poverty, which one reaches as a landing place from this human failure, which has a positive outlet. We thus have the passage from pure negativity to positivity. At the beginning there is revolt against God (cf. Ps 88: the psalmist rebels against God); think of the prayers of Jeremiah, who in a certain sense mistreats God: “You are to me like a deceitful brook” (Jer 15:18). At the beginning there is revolt, because the believer, by the fact of having the gift of faith, is not embalmed, but remains living flesh like other people who have no faith, and is oppressed like them by the realities of life; there is revolt against God and against reality, but then a gradual acceptance arises, which begins to take over with what I would call the interior silence of the soul. Think of Ps 131, very short, but very suggestive:

“O Lord, my heart is not lifted up,
my eyes are not raised too high;
I do not occupy myself with things
too great and too marvelous for me.
But I have calmed and quieted my soul,
like a weaned child with its mother;
my soul is like the weaned child that is with me.
O Israel, hope in the Lord
from this time on and forevermore.”

After the revolt the believer returns to himself and finds his own interior settling. Finally one stakes everything on God alone against false human securities (cf. Ps 18:3: “O Lord, my rock, my fortress, my deliverer”). One arrives at God, discovered as the pivot of our existence, of our life. Thus one reaches the joyful and savory experience, tasted, of one’s own nothingness. The supreme expression of this spirituality will be Mary and Jesus. Mary with her total silence. She, with her unconditional availability to God, is an existential silence, but not a silence of emptiness, of absence, rather a silence of full presence to the Lord at the moment when she dissolves into the most complete silence of herself. Mary, in the account of the announcement of the messianic motherhood, is presented as availability made person before God, which makes possible the effectiveness and fruitfulness of the greatest divine call in history after that of Christ. Jesus will say: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, ...learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt 11:28-29). Matthew thus renders the term “poor”, splitting it into “gentle” and “humble in heart”; a binary expression that connotes the one who is truly poor, the poor of God: Jesus made obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Introduction

Precisely because our course is entirely centered on the prayer of the poor of God in the Bible, we now want to see the obstacles to this ideal, to the attainment of this spiritual identity. If the soul of the biblical poor man is the stripping away of all human securities, of all human self-sufficiency, the obstacles to acquiring this soul will be those that give citizenship to these elements, that is, everything that can nourish or give birth to self-sufficiency. There is, in fact, also spiritual self-sufficiency, the attitude of those who think themselves righteous and about whom we have a few words in the Gospel.

1. The Intellectual Temptation

The first obstacle to the authentic biblical soul is the intellectual temptation. It consists in identifying certain elements that give body to prayer with prayer itself. Obviously when we speak of prayer we are not speaking of pure sentimentalism, of fine ready-made phrases. God continues to speak to his people and the Bible is the word of God, not in an exhaustive sense, but in the normative sense of the term. This means that every word of God must be measured against the one contained in the Bible. God, in fact, speaks also and above all in our life, through the events that weave its fabric. The word of God starts from Scripture, but becomes authentic, substantial and alive when it reaches our life and is expressed in life. God speaks to us through our daily lives, in the events of our everyday, which become word of God, which must however be measured by the criterion of the Bible.

We understand, then, that prayer, to be serious, must have content, but one cannot identify prayer with the ideas that give body to prayer itself. Prayer is not a moment in a course of theology, nor a moment of learned dissertation; it is rather a state of soul, a moment of life in which we conform our will and our plans to those of God. Let us think of the prayer of Jesus, about which the Gospels will shortly tell us something: it is condensed in practice in the expression: “Your will be done”. The Psalms are a luminous example of authentic prayer. In psalmic prayer, in fact, God is always at the center, never man and much less man’s thoughts; but always and only in the foreground is the presence of the God who acts rather than of the God who is thought about. This is why all psalmic prayer is centered on adoration and gratitude. Adoration, whose object is the greatness of God and our weakness; gratitude, whose object is the goodness of God and our trust in him.

Prayer is therefore the language of the heart, but of the “heart” in the biblical sense, not in the modern sense of “feeling”. “Heart”, in fact, in the Bible says much more, because it connotes the whole interior of man, the “deep self” of modern psychology. So to speak of prayer as the language of the heart is not to speak of a pious religious sentiment, still less of religious sentimentalism. In prayer, when it is authentic, we have the best expression of ourselves, because our prayer always reflects ourselves, what we really are, both our authenticity and our inauthenticity. And if in prayer we play a part with God, this means that we behave in this way with Him in life too. For this reason one can say: “Tell me the prayer you have and I will tell you who you are”. Prayer is the language of the heart in the deep sense.

In a religious perspective prayer is the expression of our faith, it is a moment of emergence, of faith coming to the surface. Prayer is a crossing of gazes in the deep sense, of the gaze of life. It is the gaze that a person casts and that reveals him; certain dialogues take place more through the meeting of gazes than through an exchange of words. Therefore to pray means to learn to look at God and to let oneself be looked at by Him, to learn to love Him and to let oneself be loved by Him. We too often identify our prayer with the saying of formulas or with our doing something. We like to feel ourselves the protagonists in prayer and of our prayer. This is a rationalistic concept of prayer, a Pelagian concept and scarcely evangelical. If prayer is a dialogue of life with God, in dialogue there are always two who speak, otherwise one has a monologue.

2. The Temptation of Feeling

A second obstacle to the soul of the “biblical poor man” is the temptation of feeling. It is a classic error to confuse good prayer with prayer that is felt. If prayer is an encounter with God, it is essentially dialogue with God, a relationship of life with Him, and all this means highly vital, lived and therefore experiential realities. One prays not in order to find oneself, but in order to give oneself, as happens in every authentic interpersonal encounter. True prayer is the kind that puts us in tune with God not only at the level of feelings, but of lived life, at the level of the will. What counts is not so much the type of prayer, but the object of this experience, that is, beloved God who absorbs us totally. Therefore in prayer we must know how to lose ourselves in order to find ourselves again in Him, transformed by his active presence. God is always present, always active; there is no passive God, in which case we would have only an idol. The word “idol” comes from the Greek and means that which only appears. The God of divine Revelation, our God, is a God always present, always active for us as well as with us. Now prayer has precisely this God as its object: beloved God who must absorb us totally. Prayer is therefore a finding ourselves again in Him, transformed by his active presence.

Let us think of the prayer of the tax collector and that of the Pharisee (Luke 18:9-14). The Pharisee was a committed religious man of his time. The Pharisees, in fact, were those who today in the Church of God are the men and women religious, the consecrated, those committed to an intense, integral and totalizing religious life for God. But this way of life had also brought with it an improper way of thinking. The Pharisees considered themselves God’s creditors, because they were convinced that they had given and were giving much to God. The tax collector, on the other hand, was a customs official of the time, a category regarded as thieves by trade. Now in the parable the real thief becomes the Pharisee, not the tax collector, precisely at the moment when he is parading his own merits before God and making himself a creditor; in this way he is robbing God of all his glory, because he thinks that he is the one doing something, he thinks that he is the one doing everything the good God has permitted him to do, he thinks that he is the one who has given to God, whereas he has only received, like every man who comes into this world. The tax collector, on the other hand, there at the back of the temple, does not dare to lift his head; at that moment he has no awareness of giving, indeed he is there to confess that he has been a thief, but in fact he makes God a most beautiful gift, he gives God the gift of the possibility of forgiving him, and the roles are reversed.

3. The Temptation of Action

The third obstacle is the temptation of action. I would say that it is the specific temptation of today. We live in a climate of efficiency-mania and consumerism. Today, instinctively, the criterion of evaluation we have is not related to the goodness in itself of things, but depends on their efficiency. A thing is worth something not if it is good in itself, but if it goes on the market; therefore consumerism is paradoxically inversely proportional to the value of the things themselves.

And this temptation of action, in our case, shows itself in the question: “What do I do while I pray?”. Today there is difficulty in understanding the value of prayer in life, even on the part of believers. In the Gospel we have a whole series of parables of waiting or of vigilance, which give us the most authentic attitude of man: knowing how to place ourselves before God by first accepting our poverty as creatures. We give God nothing; it is He who in reality does everything for us; it is already a great deal when we let God act. Our doing, at bottom, is essentially and primarily to be sincere and honest, it is to remove the obstacles that prevent God from acting in us. Knowing how to accept our poverty as creatures and knowing how to let God work in us, for us and with us — this presupposes a great deal, because the obstacles we must remove daily in order to let God act are so many and so great.

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps 127:1). It is the Lord who builds our city, God always works, even if he often works in silence, and when God is silent it is a sign that then he is working a great deal in us and for us, more than when he makes himself heard. Let us think of the Gospel episode of Jesus in the boat (Mark 4:31-41). He sleeps, yet he is very much present. The obstacles take concrete form for us in the lack of interior silence, but of that interior silence that means the dismantling of ourselves before God. The opposite of this, instead, is the disordered attachment to our ideas and our plans, the conviction that it is we who act, who do, that God must behave in this or that way, that He cannot ask this or that, that God cannot think in any way other than the one we judge.

A God whose ways of thinking we foresee is not the true God, he is rather an idol. Our God is the true God, because he is immensely imaginative and unpredictable. Our God of yesterday is not the God of today and will not be the God of tomorrow. And consequently this disordered attachment to our preconceived ideas about Him is an expression of our lack of trust in God. We do not trust Him and consequently we find it hard to hang the cloak of our life on God’s hook. We are too attached to the ideal picture we have made of ourselves, of God, of religious life, in the sense of life of faith, of believing life. We should remember what we are told and what is attributed to St. Teresa of Avila: “When you accept in peace the trial of not pleasing yourself, then you will make room for Christ”.

Introduction

Let us now see how Jesus was the living, complete, absolute, unattainable incarnation of this soul of the “poor of God”. In the NT it turns out that Jesus is the “poor of God” par excellence, because he is the favorite Son and therefore, as such, he is the perfect transparency of the Father. “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

1. Jesus, the “Messiah of the Poor” in the OT

It was above all the phenomenon of the exile that marked the definitive orientation of the messianic conception of the people of God. Before the exile the messianic orientation was predominantly political. It was thought that the future Messiah would be an ideal king, seeing that historically the kings who had succeeded one another had always disappointed the people’s expectations. With the exile came the experience of the annihilation of all of Israel’s sacred institutions, an extremely serious fact in a cultural context of theocracy, where God was understood as the absolute foundation of society. In this spiritual climate the figure of the Messiah develops as the living expression of the servant of God; thus an eminently religious, spiritual perspective is born. The servant of God par excellence, the poor of God will be the supreme personification of this spirituality, the spirituality of the purified Israel. Thus the exile and the post-exilic period make the people of Israel concretely experience what the Prophets had foretold about the famous “remnant”: what saves the mass is the small faithful group that remained within it, which acts as leaven in the midst of the dough. In Amos 3:12 the prophet says: “Thus says the Lord: As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the people of Israel be rescued who live in Samaria...”. Then in v. 15: “I will tear down the winter house as well as the summer house... the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall come to an end, says the Lord.” The mass is thus swept away and only the prophetic “remnant” remains.

From this sifting the best remains, the fine flour, the remnant of Israel. This experience, obviously, is of an ecclesial dimension. Using Pauline language, we could say that it is the new Israel, the true Israel. Why? Because the poverty of the restoration after the return from exile was inadequate to the hopes that had been conceived. Isa 41:14-16 bears witness to this:

“Do not fear, you worm Jacob,
you insect Israel!
I will help you, says the Lord;
your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.
Now, I make of you a threshing sledge, new,
sharp, and having teeth;
you shall thresh the mountains and crush them,
and you shall make the hills like chaff.
You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away,
and the tempest shall scatter them.
Then you shall rejoice in the Lord;
in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory.”

Thus these people, in this situation of extreme material, social, political and spiritual poverty, feel themselves redeemed. We have heard Isaiah speak of Redeemer: “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel”. The theme returns again in Isa 51:11: “So the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing”. They are ransomed, they are poor, but “poor of God” in a religious perspective, because freed by him: “Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the Lord has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his suffering ones” (Isa 49:13). It is the Lord who sets free, and therefore the faithful feel themselves servants of God, disciples of the Lord in a deep, spiritual, genuine sense, because they hope in him alone inasmuch as they feel that they have God’s law in their own hearts. When everything human is shattered, God can enter and take space: “Listen to me, you who know righteousness, you people who have my teaching in your hearts” (Isa 51:7). We have the parallelism between “righteousness” and “my teaching” (my law); here, therefore, “righteousness” is not to be understood in the sense of our modern vocabulary, that is, giving each one his due, but in the sense of biblical righteousness, which means doing what God asks, being expert in carrying out the will of God.

And the Messiah will be this ideal servant of God, he will be the prototype of this service of God and therefore will be felt to be the Messiah of this type of poor. In fact the figure of the Messiah is now no longer that of a king, but that of the servant of God, a figure that is born precisely in this cultural and environmental climate. We have two testimonies in this regard: one from Isaiah and the other from Zechariah. As for Isaiah, we must recall the famous four songs or poems of the Servant of God, in which there is the oracle and the messianic investiture of the future Messiah:

“Listen to me in silence, O coastlands;
let the peoples renew their strength; let them draw near...
Here is my servant, whom I uphold,
my chosen, in whom my soul delights;
I have put my spirit upon him;
he will bring forth justice to the nations...” (cf. Isa 41:1; Isa 42:1;)
“Listen to me, O coastlands,
pay attention, you peoples from far away!
The Lord called me before I was born,
while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
He made my mouth like a sharp sword,
in the shadow of his hand he hid me.” (Isa 49:1-6).

Here we have the account of the Servant’s vocation. Finally, in the third song (Isa 50:4-11) we have a confession of the servant in the style of the famous confessions of Jeremiah:

“The Lord God has given me the tongue of a teacher,
that I may know how to sustain the weary
with a word.”

The Lord has given him, that is, a tongue that knows how to speak competently of the will of God, that knows how to mediate adequately the message that God entrusts to him. In Isa 52:13-53:12 we have the fourth poem, which is practically the account of the passion in preview.

Let us see the import of these texts. First of all, the four songs unfold in a humble climate: the Messiah will not come with human power, he will not rely on human efficiency. Let us recall Paul’s testimony about his apostolic experience in 1 Cor 2:2-3: “I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling... For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified”.

The same thing, long before, was done by the Servant of God: he trusted in God alone, he used the discretion and humility of God, who speaks through his Spirit. A Calvinist theologian in one of his books defines the Holy Spirit as the “humility of God”. In fact the authentic Spirit makes no noise, is discreet, speaks in a low voice, so that attention and silence are needed in order to hear him. The first spiritual constant of these songs is therefore that of a humble, discreet ministry, the humility and discretion of God, and then on the human side we have the constant of the martyrdom of the Redeemer, of this Servant of God. The Messiah will live his mission by paying in person to the very end and accepting death out of fidelity to his own mission, out of fidelity to God, out of fidelity to human beings. The historical motivation of this figure so painted in the texts of Isaiah about the servant of God is, as we said, the humble and disappointing situation of the post-exilic period; it was a laborious, humble and disappointing reconstruction. The conviction was nevertheless maintained that God’s plan would succeed, that God could not fail, could not be defeated, but that he would fulfill his promises in a future man through the efficacy of his martyrdom.

Life always succeeds through death and rises again from death. In the post-exilic period the prophets, since they will be the only load-bearing structure of the people, will also constitute Israel’s only point of reference. Hence the Messiah will be seen as a prophetic figure in the texts of the Songs of the Servant of God. This Messiah is seen as a prophet: he preaches, he proclaims justice to the nations, etc... “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people”, says Moses in the name of God (Deut 18:15). In the line of Moses and Jeremiah and like them, the future Servant of God will be an intercessor, an instrument of intercession:

“Therefore I will allot him a portion with the great,
and he shall divide the spoil with the strong;
because he poured out himself to death,
and was numbered with the transgressors;
yet he bore the sin of many,
and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isa 53:12).

Therefore he will be a great intercessor between God and the people and, moreover, he will be the servant of the word (Isa 42:4). In the other poems too this theme is quite common:

“He will faithfully bring forth justice” (Isa 42:3).

Here “justice” always indicates God’s will for us made manifest by the Servant.

“He will not grow faint or be crushed
until he has established justice in the earth;
and the coastlands wait for his teaching.”

It is a matter of doctrine, of teaching; he will therefore be the servant of the word of God, he will fight against sin, he will be a sign of contradiction to the point of being led to death (Isa 50:4-9). Moreover, he will be in intimate dialogue with God:

“Listen to me, O coastlands,
pay attention, you peoples from far away!
The Lord called me before I was born,
while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
He made my mouth like a sharp sword,
in the shadow of his hand he hid me;
he made me a polished arrow,
in his quiver he hid me away...” (Isa 49:1-6).

Here we have stated the Servant’s intimacy with God and his availability even to martyrdom. Therefore, as one can see, here is the spirituality of the “poor of God”, which evokes the man bowed down, because dismantled, because he is poor and has nothing, who has let himself be annihilated, emptied.

After the poems of the Servant of God we have the oracle of Zechariah, a text that Matthew will cite for Jesus’ triumphal entry into Jerusalem:

“Rejoice greatly, O daughter Zion!
Shout aloud, O daughter Jerusalem!
Lo, your king comes to you;
triumphant and victorious is he,
humble and riding on a donkey,
on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
He will cut off the chariot from Ephraim
and the war horse from Jerusalem;
and the battle bow shall be cut off,
and he shall command peace to the nations;
his dominion shall be from sea to sea,
and from the River to the ends of the earth” (Zech 9:9-10).

In Zechariah the Messiah reappears as a figure of King. Precisely because the prophet foretells the future Messiah in this oracle, it is a triumphal hymn to the Messiah in his city. But we must note the difference between this type of king and the king Messiah conceived in the pre-exilic period. Here he does not appear with the sumptuous apparatus of the king of the time, who went on horseback; he uses, rather, the humble mount of the ancient Bedouin chiefs, the donkey. Moreover, he is qualified in Hebrew as “humble”, that is, gentle and meek. The background is that of the Servant of God: he will proclaim justice, peace to the nations.

2. Jesus, “Messiah of the Poor” in the NT

Let us now see in the NT the new fulfillment in Jesus of this expectation. Jesus fully realizes in his earthly life this ideal of spiritual poverty, as total availability in the hands of the Father, through humility, meekness and crystalline gentleness. Here lies the core of spiritual poverty: total, unconditional availability in the hands of the Father. Availability that is expressed in humility, in meekness, in gentleness.

The temptation of Jesus in the desert too must be seen in this light, in this framework. The messianic expectations of the time were predominantly political. They were under Roman rule and so they awaited a Messiah who would redeem them from the foreign yoke. Hence Jesus has this impassioned confrontation with his own vocation after the intense experience of his baptism. To speak of Jesus tempted in the desert means to speak of his profound interior experience about the meaning of his own mission. Jesus perceives, on the one hand, the type of messianism that the Father wants from him, which is that in the line of the Servant of God; at the same time, however, he is urged on by another voice, which declares itself to come from God, because it is that of the official religion of his environment. The Apostles had to learn this experience of his from Jesus himself.

We know what happened at Caesarea Philippi! Jesus, at a certain point in his life, wants to place his disciples clearly before the realization of who he is. First he asks: “Who do people say that I am?”, then, when he sees that they are well informed, he says: “But who do you say that I am?”. And Peter, in the name of the group, answers (cf. Mark 8:27-30). Then Jesus immediately begins to correct their messianic outlook. In fact, when he begins to foretell the Passion for the first time, Peter is scandalized and Jesus answers violently: “Get behind me, Satan!” (Mark 8:33). Jesus then begins to catechize them with the three announcements of the Passion, common to Matthew, Mark and Luke. After each announcement of the Passion there is always a short passage on discipleship: the invitation to become like children, to be last if one wants to be first, to be servants if one wants to rule, etc... We have the following of the self-expropriation in the line of Christ Jesus, the Absolute expropriated by the Father out of love for human beings.

And here, then, is the meaning of the three temptations. The first concerns hunger. The Messiah cannot suffer, because in the Jewish theological mentality suffering is the fruit of sin, it is the sinner who is struck, who suffers; the just man cannot be struck and suffer. This is the great question of the whole book of Job. And so the devil urges him on the matter of suffering and hunger. The second temptation: the Messiah will have to reign over Israel by means of a sign, as Moses did with the signs of the Exodus. And the devil takes Him to the pinnacle of the temple: “Throw yourself down, God will support you”. The third temptation: the Messiah will have to dominate the pagan nations. With the Messiah Israel will become ruler of the world, even of the pagans. The third temptation takes him up that very high mountain from which the whole world can be seen. It is an account narrated in a parabolic way, that is true, but where Jesus speaks of his temptation it is a matter of a real experience of Christ; therefore the account is historical not in its materiality of a filmed sequence, but is historical inasmuch as it reports a true, objective temptation lived by Christ.

Matthew narrates the account of Jesus tempted in the desert along the lines of the events of the Exodus: Jesus is presented as the new Moses and new Israel who, unlike historical Israel, remains faithful in the trial. And so Israel, the true people of God, in Jesus says its first unconditional, total yes to God. Historically God had to come all the way to Jesus in order to obtain from man the first full, total, absolute yes.

For Luke, Jesus lives his story by repeating in his experience not that of the Exodus, but that of man, of Adam in Eden. Luke is a converted pagan, therefore he is interested in man as such, not in the Hebrew. In fact he places before the account of the temptation the genealogy, which is very different from Matthew’s. In Matthew the genealogy is meant to indicate Jesus as son of David, Davidic Messiah; in Luke, instead, the genealogy indicates Jesus as son of man, the authentic, true man. Jesus, like Moses, is fully obedient to the Father for the kind of mission entrusted to him, he is the true servant of God in the line of Moses and therefore is the one who in his obedience can redeem the disobedience of Israel, because Israel in Jesus says its first full and total yes to God. In Luke’s line Jesus is the new Adam, the first historical man truly successful in his fidelity to God; because he is abandoned in fullness to the Father, He redeems humanity.

And this Jesus is the Messiah of the poor. One therefore understands why the temptation of Jesus is placed precisely at the beginning of the public life; it illuminates, in fact, the whole life of Christ, it says the fundamental orientation of his soul. The Evangelists anticipate it at the beginning and, I would say, almost exhaust this temptation at that moment, almost as if to say what was from the beginning the fundamental, decided, absolute orientation of his soul. And so Jesus defines himself as the “poor of God”: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt 11:29). The biblical “heart”, as I said above, is the deep self of the person, which embraces the whole interior and most substantial being of the individual, there where we are truly ourselves and cannot play a part either with God or with others, there where we cannot cheat anyone and there can be no half measures. Jesus has this gentle, patient and humble soul, he is the gentle and humble of heart, he is the true Servant of God, the one totally available to the Father, totally expropriated of himself for the Father and for human beings. The Father and human beings have always found in Jesus complete welcome; Jesus never refused to meet anyone; if anything, it is human beings who refused the encounter with Christ. Jesus lives as a poor man, materially he is born in a cave, he identifies himself with the poor, the unfortunate, the little ones: “Just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (Matt 25:40).

Introduction

Jesus is the one who prays par excellence, Jesus is prayer personified. In fact he is continually present to the Father and lives without interruption the presence of the Father. His life is entirely a communion lived with the Father. The last verse of the prologue of the fourth Gospel says: “No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known” (John 1:18). No one has ever seen God; it is the only-begotten Son himself, who is constantly turned and straining toward the bosom of the Father, who has revealed him. And so I like to imagine Jesus as the needle of the compass in its position continually turned to the North. Christ is as if magnetized in his person by the continual attraction toward the Father; the Father is the lung of his breathing; one may say that Jesus breathes with the lung of the Father.

1. The Praying Jesus of the Gospels

This one of John, one of the many definitions of Jesus that we find in the NT, indicates the orientation of his soul. The prayer of Jesus was not made up, as ours is, of returns to the presence of the Father, but was rather like the surfacing of the intensity with which he permanently lived this presence. Now this datum of the prayer of Christ, as of a habitual attitude of his soul, is offered to us above all by the Gospel of Luke. He is the evangelist par excellence of the praying Christ.

A brief comparative statistic among the Synoptics, Matthew, Mark and Luke, is interesting in this regard. Mark speaks three times of the prayer of Jesus or, if you like, of the praying Jesus; Matthew also speaks of it three times; Luke, on the other hand, speaks of it nine times. Let us start from Mark, the oldest Gospel, and precisely from Mark 1:35. We are after the famous “day at Capernaum”.

It must be remembered that the evangelists did not give us biographies of Christ. The Gospels are not biographies of Jesus, but presentations of his figure, of the saving meaning of Christ, so that today one realizes that it is not possible to write a biography of Jesus. The Gospels, however, do not invent, but use biographical material about Christ to give us the preaching of the early Church about his Person. If we wish, we can say that the Gospels are four strands, four different preachings of the early Church about Jesus, about the person of Christ, and this is immensely richer.

In this perspective Mark presents a typical day of Jesus. At the end of this day He withdraws to pray: “In the morning, while it was still very dark, he got up and went out to a deserted place, and there he prayed” (Mark 1:35). The second reference to the praying Jesus in Mark comes after the first multiplication of the loaves, which he has in common with Matthew: “When evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. After saying farewell to them, he went up on the mountain to pray” (Mark 6:46). And then we have the prayer in Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-39).

Matthew has in common with Mark both the prayer of Jesus after the first multiplication of the loaves (Matt 14:23) and the prayer in Gethsemane (Matt 26:36-44), also present in Luke (Luke 22:39-46). There are therefore four references to the praying Jesus in Matthew and Mark and nine in Luke. Moreover, it should be observed that Mark and Matthew present us with moments of Christ’s prayer, whereas Luke, every time he speaks of the praying Jesus, speaks of him as one caught in a situation of prayer. Think of the Baptism of Jesus (3:21-22) and the experience of his transfiguration (9:28-29). Of the latter it is said that Jesus took with him Peter, James and John, went up the mountain to pray, and that he was praying when he was transfigured, that while he was praying the appearance of his face changed. Again, Jesus prays before choosing the twelve (Luke 6:12-16). Luke shows how the twelve, the foundation of the new people of God, are born of the prayer of Christ; the Church is born of the praying Jesus. The roots of the Church are Christ Jesus and Him at prayer. The same situation holds for the origin of the Our Father. Jesus is praying, alone, and, coming out of his own prayer, he comes toward the disciples. Then they, fascinated by this Jesus who radiates prayer, say: “Teach us also to pray!” and Jesus teaches them the Our Father. Note the difference in the context of the Our Father in Matthew and in Luke. We are in Chapter 11 of Luke. In Matthew, on the other hand, the Our Father is born of the teaching Jesus, from the teaching of the new Moses who goes up the mountain. As one who teaches sits in the teacher’s chair, for Matthew Jesus goes up the new Sinai, gives his new law. In Luke, instead, the Our Father is born of the praying Jesus. The Our Father, prayer of the Church, is born of the prayer of the praying Christ. The whole ecclesial reality, the prayer of the Church, the faith of the Church, the foundations of the Church (the Twelve), are born of the prayer of Christ, and this is to say that the Church is truly the historical prolongation of the person of Christ.

2. Prayer as the Interior Attitude of Christ

Jesus is not so much one who prays as a constant prayer; therefore He is not simply a man of prayers, but of prayer, he does not pray much, but he prays always. The essence of prayer is to address God and to let oneself be addressed by Him in order to discover his will and adhere to it with love in communion of life with Him, in the fullest sense of the term “life”. Here we take the term “life” not only as movement and activity, but as the complete fitting together of two existences through their full fusion. Prayer, we know, is dialogue, and dialogue not so much of words as of vital attitude.

Jesus was shaped and as if woven of these vital attitudes of soul in adherence to the Father, and in this sense He was a teacher of prayer not so much by what he said about it, but above all by his example and by the model of one who prays that He is. This datum is fundamental, precisely because prayer is essentially a vital fact and not simply a ritual one; it is assimilated by living it and by seeing it lived. Prayer is assimilated by living it. We could say that in the Gospel of Luke we have an exemplary, normative manifestation of the praying soul of Jesus. Let us think of the twelve-year-old Jesus, who remains in the Temple and who, when he is found by Mary and Joseph, gives an answer that denotes the attitude of his soul: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49). Luke, significantly, places this episode at the beginning of the life of Christ to say the decided and constant orientation of his soul. At twelve Jesus now comes of age from the religious point of view, that is, before God; on this level he is therefore now officially and fully responsible for his acts. Luke tells us in what way Jesus presents himself as responsible before God from the very beginning of his majority, of his religious life: “I must be about my Father’s affairs”. And such will be the orientation of his whole life.

It is above all John who tells us this aspect of the soul of Christ. Jesus grasps himself and lives constantly according to the plan that the Father has for him. There are no fractures or dichotomies, that double I that is normally in us. Jesus sees and defines the Father almost always as “the One who sent him”. See John 6:37-38: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away; for I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me”. Likewise the Father in John is very many times called “the One who sent him” or “the One who sent the Son”. Obviously, by correspondence, Jesus grasps himself as “the One whom the Father sent”. The two definitions of God and of Jesus are complementary, they refer to each other, imply each other, postulate each other, and Jesus sees his whole self and his existence as the carrying out of the Father’s saving plan for humanity. He grasps himself in his deepest identity as the plan that God is carrying out for the salvation of humanity. We are still in the discourse on the bread and it is logical that he should say in this discourse: “Very truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is my Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John 6:32-33); “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty” (John 6:35).

Jesus, by the way in which he lives, is the salvation of human beings, he is the instrument of life in the hands of the Father. He has the precise awareness that his life is constantly marked by the progressive carrying out of the Father’s will; he feels that he does not have his existence as his own, that he cannot manage it by his own criteria, but that it is set to the rhythm of the Father’s will for him, by God’s deadlines. Jesus knows that it cannot be He who sets his own deadlines, but that his existence comes from the Father.

This in John is accentuated with the famous theme of the “hour”. Hence the frequent expressions: “My hour has not yet come”, “When the hour comes”, “Behold, the hour has come”. This “hour” is not merely a manner of speaking; in John it is a very strong theological theme. The “hour of Jesus” coincides with the hour of his death on the Cross, and death on the Cross in John is not seen as a capitulation of Christ, it is rather a glorious death, it is his enthronement. The Cross is the throne on which Christ is enthroned: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32). And here the verb “to lift up” has a twofold meaning: the physical one, that is, that Jesus is lifted up on the Cross, and the theological one, that is, that Jesus is sublimated, raised up and exalted, because he fully realizes what he is: “So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice” (John 16:22). And he gives the example of the woman: “When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come. But when her child is born, she no longer remembers the anguish because of the joy of having brought a human being into the world. So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice” (John 16:21-22). Here Jesus speaks of the hour of childbirth as the hour of the woman, to say that it is in motherhood that she fully realizes herself, that life is truly life when it is not sterility but fruitfulness; a sterile life is death, since life is essentially growth, is development.

Likewise for Jesus the hour of his death is “his hour” in the sense that Jesus finds himself again in fullness precisely in his complete yes to the Father and to human beings. Jesus does not passively undergo his own death, but manages it responsibly, because in the death that human beings inflict on him, He, without any coercion, says his fullest yes to the Father and his most total yes to human beings. It is a yes of fidelity to his mission, with which He identifies himself, and therefore it is also a yes of fidelity to himself. And that is why that is “his hour” by definition, the one that marks the life of Christ and the one of which He has a lucid awareness. This awareness is fully accepted by Him and made totally his own, nourished and lived to the end.

Now it is precisely this interior universe of Christ that gives substance to all his prayer. Jesus, in the truest way, is this habitual, daily communion with the Father, Jesus is this transparent presence to the Father, not only at the level of feelings and reflective consciousness, but above all at the level of life concretely lived. In this sense Jesus is the great one who prays and is the supreme model, the incarnate teaching of authentic Christian prayer.

Introduction

We now wish to see the same datum of the “praying Christ” grasped from the side of concrete lived experience, and to listen for this purpose to the Gospels telling us of the prayers of Jesus as revealing indicators of the quality of his prayer, telling us of the fabric of his praying soul. These prayers always present us with Jesus praying his own life; we therefore see in Jesus an incarnate prayer, which is born of life and expresses it. It is not only a prayer that is inserted into his life as one moment among many, but a prayer that is born of his life and expresses it. We therefore wish to see, in two moments, the prayers concerning the mission of Christ and then the prayers concerning directly his life.

1. Prayers Concerning His Mission

A first text presents us with Jesus who “went out to the mountain to pray; and he spent the night in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles: Simon, whom he named Peter, and his brother Andrew, and James, and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James son of Alphaeus, and Simon, who was called the Zealot, and Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor” (Luke 6:12-16). This reference to the prayer of Jesus in Luke tells us that He prays before choosing the twelve, because it is a decisive moment of his messianic activity, inasmuch as Jesus with the choice of the Twelve is laying the foundations of the new people of God; that is why he chooses twelve: they are to constitute a kind of historical replica of the twelve Patriarchs of the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus with his messianic activity inaugurates the new “people of God”, that of the “last times”. It is not, however, a radically new people that has nothing to do with the preceding one. In himself Jesus came for Israel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt 15:24). Obviously God’s promises can never know failure and therefore the radius has been widened with the opening to all who will believe, but without the exclusion from the new people of God of historical Israel, which in fact had excluded itself by its refusal.

The Twelve, therefore, are the twelve new Patriarchs of the new universal people of God.

For this reason after Easter we see the concern to reconstitute the group, now lacking a member with Judas’s departure. Peter then takes the floor and declares this necessity in a programmatic way (Acts 1:21-22). Here too one first prays and the choice is left to God; they cast lots and let God do the choosing. As we see, the early Church does nothing but imitate the Master. This prayer of Christ, for its part, tells us that we are before a Jesus who is always in constant search of what pleases God. Jesus shows himself as one who is acting under the impulse of the Father and at the same time is in the attitude of asking for divine assistance upon the future leaders of the new people of God whom he is about to choose.

Another symptomatic episode is that of the messianic confession at Caesarea Philippi. Let us listen to the version of Luke 9:18-21: “Once when Jesus was praying alone, with only the disciples near him...”. Note that Jesus prays alone; never in the Synoptics is Jesus presented at prayer with others. “...he asked them, ‘Who do the crowds say that I am?’ They answered, ‘John the Baptist; but others, Elijah; and still others, that one of the ancient prophets has arisen.’ He said to them, ‘But who do you say that I am?’ Peter answered, ‘The Messiah of God.’” Here too Christ prays before eliciting the messianic confession.

This confession represents, according to the Gospels, a kind of watershed in the messianic life of Jesus. One could say that everything tends toward this moment and everything unfolds from this moment onward. The datum is evident above all in Mark, where the whole structure of the Gospel turns on this event. Jesus, who by his way of acting stirs up questions in the crowd, in the leaders of the people, in the twelve, at a certain point takes the initiative and makes the twelve say who he truly is. In the subsequent part of the Gospel Jesus then restricts all his messianic activity to the Twelve, because by now the leaders of the people no longer listen to him, nor do the crowds follow him. From this moment on we have a Jesus who devotes himself above all to explicit catechesis on his own messianic identity and gives a clear discourse on the end that awaits him. Hence the three announcements of the Passion. The number three says perfection, totality, completeness. Here we have three announcements to connote the clarity and insistence with which Jesus speaks to his own about his approaching and tragic end.

As we have already seen, in the three Synoptics the three announcements of the Passion are always followed by three short literary units concerning the following of the disciple. In Luke the discourse is less clear than in Mark, because of the presence of the great journey of Jesus to Jerusalem, in which the evangelist includes a large part of Christ’s catechetical material. This way of presenting things by the evangelists underscores in this event the explicit stand taken by the Twelve toward Jesus.

As for the prayer of Christ, it is evident that in this event it still appears as a prayer in search of the Father’s will. Jesus seeks what the Father wants, what is pleasing to Him. Moreover, as in the preceding prayer, Jesus presents to the Father his request on behalf of the faith of the twelve, he begs the Father to give them the strength needed for their full adherence to the Messiah. Now it is a matter of asking for help to be able to live this faith, which they will shortly have to witness. Jesus, in fact, will put this still imperfect and embryonic faith of theirs into crisis, correcting its mistaken trajectories.
