We have, finally, a text to which I allude briefly: Luke 22:31-32. Jesus at the Last Supper says he has prayed for Peter: “Simon, Simon, listen! Satan has demanded to sift all of you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your own faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers”. Here too we have the same type of prayer. Therefore those few references to the praying Jesus or to the prayers of Jesus that we find in the Gospel of Luke concern precisely a Jesus who prays his mission, a Jesus whose prayer has as its object the Father’s plan for him and who has recourse to the experiential book of his own mission in order to make it the object of his conversation with the Father.

2. Prayers Concerning More Directly His Life

Let us now see the prayers of Jesus in which there is a more direct emphasis on his life and which therefore concern more directly his personal existence. We have first of all the reference to Jesus who is at prayer at the moment of his Baptism (Luke 3:21-22). Luke recounts the episode or event of the Baptism of Christ in a very succinct way, in only two verses, which nevertheless have a formidable theological density: “Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, ‘You are my Son, the Beloved; with you I am well pleased.’”

At the act of Baptism Luke presents Jesus in a situation of prayer, Jesus who is praying while he receives Baptism, not a Jesus who enters into prayer in order to receive it. This situation of prayer of Jesus at the moment of his Baptism is well understood if we think of the motive that drove Him to the Jordan. The movement of the Baptist was a movement of call to God and had the negative aspect of conversion, of purification for those who were in sin, but it also had the positive aspect of further drawing near to God. Jesus, wherever there was a call to the Father, to God, ran; He was of an extremely intense religiosity and therefore runs to the Jordan precisely out of this need for an ever further immersion in the Father; everything that in his environment religiously stimulates him in this direction always finds Him in first place.

The voice from heaven that we have in Luke and in Mark is revealing in this sense: we could say that it is a line of this prayerful dialogue between Jesus and the Father at that intensely religious moment. It is precisely this prayer of his that frames and contains the experience, so radical and determining, that marks a decisive turning point in his life. In Baptism, which appears as the inaugural moment and the beginning of his public life, Jesus decisively becomes aware of what the Father asks of him.

It is in this sense that the baptismal experience of Jesus presents itself as normative for us. Indeed our own baptismal experience too must constitute our primordial and true experience of God, the awareness of an incarnate, concrete God, who always presents himself to us joined to the plan of life that he offers us to live; it is always a God who demands commitment, who enters the flesh of our existence and leads us to react positively before Him.

A second prayer is that of Gethsemane, and we take it here too from Luke, moving on to chap. 22. A comparison between Matthew and Mark brings out a great divergence. “He came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives; and the disciples followed him. When he reached the place, he said to them, ‘Pray that you may not come into the time of trial.’ Then he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, knelt down, and prayed, ‘Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; yet, not my will but yours be done.’ [Datum exclusive to Luke:] Then an angel from heaven appeared to him and gave him strength. In his anguish he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground. When he got up from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping because of grief, and he said to them, ‘Why are you sleeping? Get up and pray that you may not come into the time of trial’” (Luke 22:41-44).

Let us make a few clarifications about this text, in which every word has a remarkable doctrinal charge. This prayer of Jesus possesses a universal dimension. In Luke it appears not only as the prayer of Jesus, but becomes the prayer of all the disciples. It must be remembered that the accounts of the Passion, in the intention of the evangelists, do not have a purely narrative, historical purpose, but possess a catechetical aim. The point is to propose Jesus as a model for a Church that is already experiencing persecution. In Mark and Matthew there is the reference to Jesus’ terror of death; think of the phrase: “I am deeply grieved, even to death” (Matt 26:38; Mark 14:34). In Luke this detail is not there, but in its place there is something more interesting: we have Jesus who, in agony, is in continuous tension toward the Father’s will. It was a moment of interior tension that engaged his whole Person in the imminence of this supreme moment to be lived.

In Mark 14:36, then, there is: “Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want”. In Luke there is not this prayer in two stages: the pressing invocation for help and then, once the terror of death has been overcome, the abandonment to the Father: “Yet, your will be done”. In Luke we have, instead, the prayer in a single stage, with the single motive and guiding thread of the Father’s will: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; yet, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42). Here is a prayer entirely centered on the search for the Father’s will and on the request for help to do this will. Therefore for Luke this is the model prayer, it is the norm of prayer for every disciple and for the whole community.

The whole concurs in saying that this prayer was a hard and strenuous struggle, in which Jesus had to engage all his strength and tension in order to fulfill the Father’s will. And the Father’s will appeared to Jesus very far from human plans, so that only from prayer did He receive the strength needed to face the hard trial of the Passion and death on the Cross. Christ’s prayer is a search for God’s will, not a request to avoid death. The Father answered this prayer in the sense that he helped Jesus to accept this death, this tragic end, as an expression of complete adherence to Him and to human beings.

Introduction

Let us now listen to the Gospels that speak to us of another incarnation of the “poor of God”: the Virgin Mary. First we shall listen to the evangelical testimony about Mary as the “poor woman of God” and then we shall see her prayer as an expression of her “poverty”, fixing our attention especially on the Magnificat as an X-ray of the soul of the Virgin.

1. Mary, the “Poor Woman of God”

Speaking of the presence of Mary in the Bible, one must first of all say that the Virgin is the immediate fruit of the spiritual richness of the OT. With this statement we touch the problem of whether and how the OT speaks of Our Lady. As regards the presence of Mary in the OT, I think that the same reasoning that is applied to the messianic prophecies holds. In them we have in fact very generic features of the future Messiah. In reality the Messiah in Jesus of Nazareth presented himself as the only-begotten Son of the Father, equal to the Father and God like the Father. Now this fact was unthinkable in the OT; one cannot therefore find in the OT texts that prove the divinity of Christ.

We could say that the same reasoning holds for Mary. One must ask in this regard by what path of the OT Mary reaches us, in order to know how the OT contains Mary in prefiguration, that is, how Mary is situated in relation to the people of Israel. And then from this perspective it must be said that Mary appears as the most authentic and fullest fulfillment of the OT itself. She is its best fruit.

Let us recall what has been said about the “poor of God” of the OT, especially those of the post-exilic period. In that period these poor constitute the qualitative element of Israel and constitute the so-called “remnant”, which alone deserves in the eyes of the prophets the title of “people of God”. We have seen, for example, how in Ps 149 these “poor” feel themselves to be the people of God:

“Sing to the Lord a new song,
his praise in the assembly of the faithful...
Let them praise his name with dancing,
making melody to him with tambourine and lyre.
For the Lord takes pleasure in his people;
he crowns the humble with victory.”

The expression “the Lord takes pleasure in his people” is still generic, but there is the second member of the synonymous parallelism, “he crowns the humble with victory”, which explains who this people of God that the Lord loves is: they are the humble, they are the poor, and it is this people that God will cultivate with care in the post-exilic period. Let us take another text, Zech 13:8-9:

“In the whole land,
says the Lord,
two-thirds shall be cut off and perish,
and one-third shall be left alive.
And I will put this third into the fire,
refine them as one refines silver,
and test them as gold is tested.”

From this oracle it emerges that God cultivates his people, purifies it, prunes his vine, cleans his vineyard. Now, Mary represents the best part of this “remnant”, its optimal expression, its final maturation and its fulfillment. Mary is the richest and most beautiful fruit of this throng of “poor of God” of the post-exilic period. Her voice, which we shall hear in the Magnificat, constitutes an admirable synthesis of this chain, of this host of people at prayer. Mary condenses in the Magnificat all the various resonances of the choirs of the Psalter, and her soul gathers in itself all the power of welcome toward God on the part of these poor, synthesizes all their boundless expectation. We shall see Mary, the Virgin of waiting, the Virgin of expectation, who creates the ideal climate so that in her Christ may take on our humanity.

A French Dominican, Fr. Bernard, as early as 1933 published a most beautiful book entitled: The Mystery of Mary. In it he states: “All the spiritual life of the ancient time, of the OT, reaches in Mary its apogee and its point of perfect maturity”. It is in this context that the scene of the announcement of the messianic motherhood to Mary acquires its full meaning, especially in the framing that Luke gives it. The account in Luke 1:26-38 represents a most dense and complete synthesis of all biblical Mariology.

The two chapters of the Gospel of the infancy according to Luke are structured like a two-leaved portal. The first comprises the announcement of the birth of the Precursor to Zechariah (Luke 1:5-25) and then the birth of the Baptist (Luke 1:57-79). The second is given by the announcement of the messianic motherhood to Mary (Luke 1:26-38) and then by the account of the birth of the Messiah himself. Luke is keen to show the very strong antithesis between the two situations. The events of the origin of the Baptist are placed in a climate of apotheosis; those of the origin of Christ, on the other hand, are found in a situation of humility, of shadow, almost of anonymity. The announcement of the birth of the Baptist is made to a priest. The announcement of the birth of Jesus, to an anonymous young girl; we only know that she is called Mary and nothing more. For the Baptist this announcement takes place in the Temple, the holiest place on earth; the announcement to Mary takes place in Nazareth, and we know the esteem in which Nazareth was held at that time! It was considered a place from which nothing good could come (cf. John 1:46). Nazareth, in fact, was a small town situated in a paganizing, contaminated area. For the announcement of the birth of the Baptist we find ourselves at the moment when Zechariah offers the incense, the culminating moment in the life of a Jewish priest. But when does the announcement to Mary take place? It is not indicated. It seems that Luke presents the origins of Christ as an antithesis to the Baptist in order to show that on the human level the latter has more showiness than Christ. In fact the Baptist was thought to be the Messiah and Jesus was not, even though the Baptist worked no miracles, whereas Jesus worked them. From this presentation of the facts and from the message enclosed in them there results, as an effect, that our mental schemes are overturned and mixed in a different way.

Here, then, is a not insignificant element of the meaning of the announcement to Mary: it underlines the nothingness and emptiness of the creature. Nazareth, this little-regarded place, indeed negatively judged; the person of Mary: a girl of the people, whose name is barely known; the moment: also diluted in chronological anonymity. All these data, in contrast to those concerning the Baptist, truly represent the nothingness and emptiness of the creature. Mary, however, constitutes with her nothingness and her emptiness the total availability of the creature before God. It is therefore not a question of a purely negative nothingness and emptiness; on the contrary, they are immensely positive, because they constitute the full openness of the creature to its own Creator.

In this perspective two clues are to be noted precisely in Luke 2: “Now there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; this man was righteous and devout, looking forward to the consolation of Israel” (v. 25). Simeon here is defined as the one who waits, who expects, and is anxious for the consolation of Israel, that is, for that consoling and re-creating salvation that God will bring to his people. A reference to the same datum is found in v. 38: “At that moment she [Anna] came, and began to praise God and to speak about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem”. The Gospel of the infancy therefore presents an anonymous crowd, from which a few strong symptomatic figures emerge, the crowd of those who wait, who await the Lord, his saving intervention, and Mary is their best expression in this openness to God, made of waiting for him, of projection and of active orientation toward him.

2. The Faith of Mary

It is significant that we find the first beatitude of the Gospel of Luke on the lips of Elizabeth, when she turns to Mary and says to her: “And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord” (Luke 1:45). Mary, the “poor woman of God”, precisely because of the type of faith she lived, is the ideal poor woman of the Kingdom. This faith of hers possesses four unmistakable characteristics.

a) Mary’s “Fiducial” Faith

Mary lived, first of all, an intense fiducial faith, which became gift and total abandonment to God, an interior disposition lived in a committed faith, which took concrete form in joyful stripping away to the point of complete expropriation of herself. Mary did not have merely a nominal faith, a faith, that is, content merely to admit that God exists, to affirm the features of God in theory.

Mary knew how to trust God at the announcement of the messianic motherhood, and the beatitude that Elizabeth addresses to her concerns precisely this blind trust of hers: “Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord”. We know of the drama that the Virgin lived through upon becoming aware of her messianic motherhood, a datum attested by the Gospel. When, however, she realized that she was in the line of God’s will, she answers without hesitation: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). There was therefore in Mary a suffered vocational acceptance, as in the case of Jesus. Unlike Zechariah, who doubts before the announcement he receives, Mary does not doubt but is in search of God’s will. Mary, just as she believed in the announcement of the messianic motherhood and at that moment trusted God, so always afterward she will trust the Word of the Lord even when she does not understand: “His mother treasured all these things in her heart” (Luke 2:51). More than “treasured”, there is in the original text the idea that Mary meditated, went on comparing, going deeper into all those things of which she had been witness and protagonist.

We must also recall the episode of the Wedding at Cana, where the figure of Mary stands out and where Jesus is presented almost obliquely (John 2:1-11). John shows Mary’s full trust in Jesus, even when Jesus gave his refusal. She does not withdraw or resign from this intervention of hers, but says to the servants: “Do whatever he may tell you” (v. 5). The Greek text contains the hypothetical nuance of hope and trust: Mary continues to trust her Son and in this way becomes in fact the monstrance of Christ’s glory, the occasion through which Christ begins to manifest his glory.

b) Mary’s “Gift/Abandonment” Faith

This fiducial faith of Mary naturally flows into the faith of gift and abandonment, a typically Lukan theme. And here are some clues that let us see this datum lived first in depth by Jesus and then traced by Mary. What I am about to say does not concern Mary directly, but Jesus. We know in any case that Luke likes to present Mary as the ideal disciple of Christ more than as his carnal Mother, a theme that St. Augustine will later take up in his time. Let us fix our attention on chap. 23 of Luke, the heart of the account of the Passion. I recall only three data exclusive to the Gospel of Luke. The women console Jesus as He, condemned, goes up toward Calvary. And here we witness a complete reversal of the situation. The scene begins with these women who come forward to console Christ and ends with Jesus who, instead, sets about consoling them, so that they, from consolers, become the consoled. We are before a Jesus who is totally expropriated of himself because he has lived always and exclusively for the Father. He never reserved his own time for himself, but always lived as total gift, and this emerges above all now, when even on the human level the individual, because of suffering, is more inclined to concentrate and fold in upon himself.

On the Cross too Jesus has no way of thinking only of himself, but is in total forgetfulness of himself in order to think only of others; He dies as he lived, and the type of his death in Luke illuminates well the life of Christ. In v. 34 Jesus prays for his executioners: “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing”. Jesus, inwardly, has already consummated his sacrifice, has already accepted his own death, has already given himself, has already fully adhered to the will of the Father, who wants him faithful to the end to his mission. Luke shows that Jesus dies praying, serene and abandoned, just as he lived: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Mary copies the example of Jesus, gives herself completely to God in faith as gift, complete abandonment of herself. At the end of the account of the announcement she says: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

c) Mary’s “Commitment” Faith

Mary, however, gives herself completely to her neighbor as well. It is with the intention of giving this message that, in my view, the scene of the announcement flows at once, in the sequence of the narrative, into that of the Virgin’s visit to Elizabeth. But already in Luke 2:33-35 there is the tacit allusion to Mary’s adherence to God’s plans for her, plans that envisage Mary’s existence as wholly oriented, like that of the Son, toward the salvation of human beings. Indeed Simeon speaks of the sword that will pierce the Virgin’s soul; it seems, then, that he alludes to her messianic motherhood and recalls her figure as mother of the suffering Messiah. In this situation her faith, which trusts totally in God by giving herself radically to him, becomes a faith of commitment.

It is not a faith tinged with fatalism or pessimism, but a faith made of intensely active commitment. We find this datum, as I said before, in the link between the account of the announcement and that of the visit to Elizabeth. It should be noted in this regard how Luke here orchestrates things narratively for the sake of a message. Zechariah receives the announcement of the birth of the Precursor, does not believe and is left mute, returns to his house in isolation and sterility. Mary receives the announcement of the messianic motherhood, believes, goes to Elizabeth and becomes the bearer of the Messiah and of the Spirit, that Spirit who permeates the whole account with his strong presence and who then bursts forth in the inspiration of the Magnificat. This contrast of chiaroscuro, of shadow and light, leaps out evidently from the narrative fabric of the two passages.

Another clue to Mary’s committed faith we find in the precious reference of Luke 2:41: “Now every year his parents went to Jerusalem for the festival of the Passover”. It was the annual pilgrimage of a religiously committed family. In the same line of thought is to be read the second Marian beatitude of Luke 11:27-28: “While he was saying this, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, ‘Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!’”, that is, blessed is she who was your mother. “But he said, ‘Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it’”, that is, carry it out, put it into practice. Jesus with this answer does not reject the beatitude toward Mary that came from that anonymous woman in the crowd, but rectifies it. Mary is blessed above all because she knew how to believe, that is, she knew how to trust God and entrust herself to Him, joyfully accepting to make of her life a realization of the Word of the Lord, of the will of God. St. Augustine insists on this dimension of the figure of Mary: “Mary, the most holy, did, yes certainly did the will of the Father, and therefore it counts for more for Mary to have been a disciple of Christ than to have been the mother of Christ. We repeat: it was for her a greater dignity and greater happiness to have been a disciple of Christ than to have been the mother of Christ” (Sermon 25:7-8; PL 46, 937-938).

In Luke 8:19-21 we have the same kind of discourse: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it”. Unlike Matthew and Mark, who bring out the repudiation that would emerge from the explicit comparison between those who at that moment listen to Jesus and his relatives, in Luke there is only praise of Mary. It is the observation of what her true relationship with Jesus consists in. The physical relationship with Christ does not count, because it depends on God. What counts, instead, is the other relationship, the only one that has real value and that is realized in personal adherence of faith. This reading results from the implicit reference and parallelism with 11:27-28.

We must also keep in mind Mary’s presence in the Upper Room (cf. Acts 1:14), that is, her religious, strong presence at the beginning of the life of the Church, just as she was present at the beginning of the public life of Christ. We have here the figure of Mary as mother of the total and integral Jesus and also under this aspect she appears as the typical expression of human welcome to the irruption of God into our life. Mary lived, then, a faith that expressed itself in the joyful expropriation of her whole self. Mary appears as one who always feels herself a debtor toward God. I believe that here lies the motivating secret of the first Lukan beatitude addressed to faithful Mary: Mary is faithful, because she knows how to trust, knows how to receive from God and is aware of only receiving.

d) Mary’s “Joyful Stripping Away” Faith

The gift of herself in the commitment of her own faith does not give Mary the awareness of feeling herself a creditor toward God, as happened with a certain type of Pharisaic religion. On the contrary, she always feels herself a debtor toward God. The Magnificat is revealing of this spiritual climate of hers, because it is born spontaneously from her soul precisely as a response to the beatitude that Elizabeth addresses to her: “Blessed is she who believed”. Mary does not shy away, but, instead of appropriating this praise, she throws it back to God, she makes the praise addressed to her at that moment by her cousin fall back upon the Lord. Indeed in the Magnificat she will say that she feels herself to be the poor one, the expropriated one of the good God, who can live because she receives day by day the portion of life and existence from the Lord. We would say with St. Bernard that she feels herself to be God’s aqueduct, the bridge, whose only function is to let pass to the other bank without retaining anything for herself. Mary feels herself totally referred to God and refers everything to Him.

Introduction

The Magnificat is a wonderful song of praise, it is the expression of a soul totally turned toward God. As regards Our Lady, we are immensely fortunate, because we have an inspired spiritual biography of her, something we do not have for all the saints, and this spiritual biography of hers is given precisely by the Magnificat.

1. Its Literary Context

To grasp all the richness of its doctrinal message one must pay attention to the point in the Gospel where Luke places it, to how he presents the canticle in itself and to how it is structured in the sequence of its contents. Let us briefly allude to its literary context as it results from present-day exegetical studies. The Magnificat comes immediately after the announcement of Mary’s messianic motherhood and after the episode of the visit to Elizabeth. It must therefore be read in the light of these two events, especially as a response to Elizabeth’s word, which proclaims the mystery of God and of Mary’s motherhood: – “‘And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me? For as soon as I heard the sound of your greeting, the child in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.’ And Mary said, ‘My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior’” – (Luke 1:43-45). The Magnificat is therefore a direct response in a particular way to the final beatitude of the account of the Virgin’s visit to Elizabeth.

2. Its Structure and Content

Its structure is very simple: it comprises an introduction, followed by two parts. The introduction we have in vv. 46-47, comprising the first two half-verses of the Canticle:

“My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.”

Note that we are in Hebrew poetry, which, unlike ours, does not use sound rhyme, but a kind of rhyme of content, a logical rhyme.

Hence the systematic use of parallelism, by which a thought is repeated twice, with some variations in the second expression in relation to the first. Here, then, is the sense of the parallelism that opens the canticle; the second half-verse: “My spirit rejoices in God my Savior” repeats in other words the same concept as the preceding sentence, so that “my soul” corresponds to “my spirit”, and “magnifies” corresponds to “rejoices”; there is a perfect correspondence. Mary, at the opening, declares that she glorifies God, that she sings the great things accomplished by Him, and then she has follow the enumeration of the reasons for which she praises the Lord.

The first part embraces vv. 48-50:

“For he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant.
Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
for the Mighty One has done great things for me,
and holy is his name.”

Here we have the personal reason for which Mary praises God, v. 50:

“His mercy is for those who fear him
from generation to generation.”

It refers to what precedes, but at the same time broadens the thought. Mary no longer thinks of the benefits she has received, but has before her gaze also those that God gives to all who fear him. Verse 50 is therefore a transitional verse between the first and the second part.

This part is made up of vv. 51-53:

“He has shown strength with his arm;
he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones,
and lifted up the lowly;
he has filled the hungry with good things,
and sent the rich away empty.”

These verses describe the way in which God intervenes in history by overturning human situations; there is the whole perspective of evangelical wisdom set against human wisdom, which is founded on efficiency, on overbearing power, on domination. The logic and wisdom of the Gospel are founded, instead, on what according to God’s criteria truly counts, on the principle that one gives life by dying, one rules by serving, one is great by becoming humble.

We have, finally, the conclusion, given by vv. 54-55:

“He has helped his servant Israel,
in remembrance of his mercy,
according to the promise he made to our ancestors,
to Abraham and to his descendants forever.”

The conclusion applies to the chosen people what has been said so far about God’s constant conduct in history. The first part has Mary as its subject; the second part has God as subject-object. It is He who displays his power, it is He who brings down, it is He who lifts up, it is He who fills with good things or sends away empty.

3. The Magnificat in the Life of Mary

Let us now see how the Magnificat is situated in the life of the Virgin. It must be said first of all that it is to be seen in the evangelical perspective in which it has been placed. Since the Gospel does not write chronicle, we believe that the claim of the Marian authenticity of the Magnificat understood in a literal sense is mistaken, as if the canticle had really been composed, as we now have it, by Mary at the precise moment of her visit to Elizabeth. In the perspective of the evangelical message the canticle says not only what Mary felt and lived in herself at that moment, but also how Mary rethought and understood that event after the resurrection. In this sense the Magnificat is an “authoritative document of Mary’s paschal meditation...” (A. Serra, Maria secondo il Vangelo, Brescia 1988, pp. 44-45). It is a most exalted profession of faith in which Mary goes out of herself and entrusts herself to God and to his plan in order to cooperate with him in the work of salvation according to the task that the Lord has entrusted to her. The Magnificat is therefore truly a reflection of her praying soul, above all in the sense that it truly came out of her soul and sprang from the living fabric of her whole existence, and not so much because it was materially composed by her in the particular circumstance of her visit to Elizabeth.

4. The Message of Prayer of the Magnificat

Let us now see the message of prayer that emerges from the Magnificat. In the first part (vv. 48-50) Mary proclaims what God did in her and sees this work of the Lord as a great deed of God; she feels herself at the center, in the heart of the history of salvation, and grasps herself as an instrument of the most resounding divine wonders. All this carries her away with admiration for God’s mercy toward her wretchedness: “He has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant”. Here Mary alludes to her state of lowliness, to her creaturely wretchedness, to the nothingness of the creature that she is, not so much to the attitude of her humble soul. Mary is not singing her own humility as a virtue, which attracted God’s favor; she sings, rather, her human, creaturely poverty.

Note that God, in the introduction (vv. 46-47), is called “Savior”, that is, he is grasped as intensely involved in our existence. Mary intensely personalizes her personal relationship with God without falling into intimism or selfishness, because in v. 50 we read: “His mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation”. Here too we have a reflection of the Virgin’s soul, we see Mary wholly absorbed and possessed by God. It is in this interior stripping away that she feels herself at the center of God’s love and of his plan, and this feeling is free and stripped of presumption, flowing rather into grateful wonder. Mary is sufficiently free with that authentic freedom of the Spirit, which allows God to use her as he wills, without her shielding herself improperly with false humility.

Through Mary and in Mary, God brings out his conduct toward all who fear him and his most proper attributes: Omnipotence, Holiness and Mercy. Holiness concerns God above all in his otherness from us, God the wholly other, God in his transcendence. To say: “Holy is his name” is equivalent to saying that He is ineffable, infinite, because the name says the person in his objective entity. To speak, therefore, of God’s name is to refer to the very person of God; here it is said that his person is Holy. In this datum Mary’s whole soul emerges, already expressed at the end of the announcement: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord”. Mary does not presume upon herself, Mary does not seek herself, does not appropriate anything, but opens herself, leans on and entrusts herself totally and solely to God. In this way she allows God to accomplish his prodigies freely in her. We have here the lived realization of that law of Salvation which Paul formulates in 1 Cor 1:27, where he says: “But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; God chose what is low and despised in the world, things that are not, to reduce to nothing things that are, so that no one might boast in the presence of God”. What Paul enunciates as a law of salvation, Mary sings in the Magnificat and in the lived reality of her own existence.

In the second part (vv. 50-53) we have Mary’s sapiential meditation on God’s action in history. Mary reads her personal experience within the broad picture of human events and grasps and celebrates with gratitude the loving and saving conduct of God. She sings, at the very moment in which she takes pleasure in contemplating it, “God’s own measure of evaluation” (S. Cipriani, La preghiera nel Nuovo Testamento. Spunti di esegesi e di spiritualità, Milano 1989, 173) of human events as the sole source of good and of life for human beings. This rapid sapiential meditation on human history in a religious perspective is entirely centered on the theme of the reversal of situations. Already in the canticle of Hannah, the outline from which the Magnificat springs, this theme is present in singing the praises of God. It is used to exalt the efficacy of the Lord’s lordship over human history. The last word on this history is spoken by God alone, not by human beings, even if at times they seem to be the winners. Inauthentic human situations will in the end be overturned, the true reality will come to the surface and appearance will vanish, the chaff will be carried away by the wind, the substantial weight of genuine grain will remain, which is given by the value judged according to God’s measure of evaluation.

For the same purpose three typical expressions of human greatness are then enumerated. Pride: “He has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts”; power: “He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly”; wealth: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty”. At bottom, they are the three constants of every human power or greatness of all times. The pride of culture, which manipulates public opinion; the pride of social position, which with arrogance opens doors that are closed to others; power, which synthesizes the two preceding; and wealth, which provides the means to impose oneself at one’s own whim. They are the classic human greatnesses closed in on themselves, three self-sufficiencies in conflict with God, and it is precisely in this orientation of theirs that their weakness and defeat lie; precisely because they are weaknesses that close themselves to God, they condemn themselves to suicide.

Mary sings this mystery of the human being and of his history, she sings the mercy of God which, having welcomed it within herself, she has experienced in depth. But at the same time she sees this saving, creative, restorative, life-giving mercy of God broadening out in concentric rays so as to embrace the whole of humanity and reach it through the mediation of the chosen people, of which she appears as the most expressive part together with her Son Jesus.

In the conclusion (vv. 54-55), with the expression: “He has helped his servant Israel, etc...”, Mary returns to the event that provoked her praise: what God did in her, the messianic motherhood, manifests the divine mercy not only toward Mary, but toward all Israel. Indeed, this fact is the chief sacramental expression of what God has done and is doing for his people. God is using Mary to carry out in favor of the chosen people the ancient promises.

Introduction

Let us now examine the evangelical message on the identity of the Christian as “poor of God”, because a child of the Kingdom. The Christian is a “poor of God” because he has the soul of the child in the sense understood by Jesus, and this datum constitutes the specific character of his identity. In fact this Christian characteristic is spoken of in those texts that give us the essential elements of the evangelical message.

1. Identity of the Christian as “Poor of God”

Let us start from the beatitude of Matt 5:3:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit,
for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

The term “spirit” in the Bible connotes “force, energy, power” and is said above all of God, because the Spirit is a good of his exclusive property that He alone can share with others. In Gen 2, when God creates man, he blows into the nostrils of this still inert being his own spirit, that is, his own breath of life. The word spirit indicates life, that is, the fundamental energy of a living being.

Therefore the “spirit of man” indicates his life and consequently means his soul in its various states; hence the expressions “spirit of hatred”, “spirit of vengeance”, “spirit of wickedness”, etc... In synthesis, the “spirit”, said of man, says the human soul in the sense of the deep self of the person. The specification “poor in spirit” indicates those who have the soul of the true poor man, who are poor before God. Whoever is not poor in this way, but is poor only on the sociological level, is in reality a potential rich man.

It is well not to forget that in the Gospels we have the ideal of radicalism for Christ, but not the ideal of poverty seen in itself. Christ did not come to preach sociological poverty, but came to redeem it, because sociological poverty is not in itself a value. Jesus declares blessed those who, on the contrary, have a humble heart, a soul bowed down before God, who know how to accept themselves as creatures of God, who do not make themselves the center of their own existence, the pivot of the whole of reality.

Matt 5:3 therefore offers the synthetic and global definition of the Christian, it helps us to understand the poverty of which it speaks in a religious sense and not in an evanescent sense. In this situation the poor man declared blessed by the Gospel is the poor man who has been helped by his socio-economic condition to welcome the gratuitousness of God, to recognize his own dependence on Him. Material poverty has only an indirect function, in the sense that, if one has not experienced the reality of life in all its crudeness, one cannot understand its just value, the value it in fact has before God.

The real, sociological poor man is therefore called blessed only to the extent that he has understood what life is, what human precariousness is, what the infinity of God is, where the true values and the secure foundation of existence lie. From all this it emerges that the word “poor” in Judaism has an intense moral, religious nuance, so that blessed are those who have before God the soul of the true poor man, those who recognize their own limits as creatures.

2. Origin of This Poverty: The Soul of the Child (Matt 18:1-4)

The origin of this identity of the Christian resides in the possession of that child’s soul as it is presented to us in Matt 18:1-4. In this chapter Matthew, in order to respond to a fundamental need of the first Christian communities, gathers together a set of sayings of Jesus, which have as their common theme fraternal life together. Note how v. 3 begins: “Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever becomes humble like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven”. This Matthean discourse of Jesus, called “ecclesiastical”, because it has the purpose of illustrating how fraternal life is to be lived in the Church, is structured in two movements. Verses 1-14 state the spiritual climate of Christian fraternity, and this is given by the type of members who compose it: it is composed of children, of little ones, evidently not in a physical and material sense. Verses 15-35 then deal with the internal life of the fraternity with its various problems: that of fraternal correction, of common prayer, of forgiveness of offenses, etc...

In this context v. 3 serves as the foundation of the exhortation to lower oneself in view of the Kingdom. “To lower oneself” means to become poor, lowly, and this implies a real change of oneself, a real transformation of one’s soul. In the verb “to become” there is the connotation of a progressive movement implied in this transformation, a change whose end result is to make one become like children. The child is taken here as a term of comparison. It is therefore important to know from what point of view the category “child” is taken. Let us say at once that it is used according to what constitutes the specific characteristic of the child. Now the specific character of the child is given by his inability to provide for himself, by the absence of self-sufficiency; the child is a personified limit and an existential dependence on others. He cannot exist without the help of others, so he is an open hand, he is receptivity personified. In this situation, asking is for the child a spontaneous fact. It is according to this perspective that Jesus takes the child as the prototype of the candidate for the experience of the Kingdom of God, that is, for the total experience of God. For it is this soul that constitutes the authentic disciple, who is such inasmuch as he knows how to live in the climate of gratuitousness, of the gift received, knows how to feel himself constantly a gift of the Father in Christ Jesus and through Christ Jesus.

3. Existential Radicalness of the Disciple’s Poverty

The datum of the believer’s objective radicalness we have in John 3:3-5. We are at the encounter with Nicodemus, who in John 3 appears as the representative of the imperfect believer. Jesus, in response to the testimony Nicodemus gives him, states: “Very truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above” (v. 3). The Italian CEI version rightly says “from above”, but the word John uses in the Greek can have a double meaning: it can mean both “anew” and “from above”. In fact Nicodemus shows that he understood Jesus’ statement in the sense of “anew”. Jesus then repeats the statement, specifying it: “Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit”. The Christian life implies a true rebirth, one must be born “anew”. But one is reborn under the impulse of God, with the absolutely necessary intervention of his Spirit.

Here, then, are the two fundamental conditions for entry into the Kingdom: the baptism of water and the re-creating work of the Spirit. As we see, we have here the idea of rebirth, but it is linked to the Synoptic theme of the child.

In John’s teaching becoming a child again consists in being reborn to a totally new life, because it is received from above and comes only from God as absolute gratuitousness. Therefore the Christian, in everything he is, in everything he can do and in everything he does, is full gratuitousness, is absolute and exclusive gift. The authentic Christian is the one who has a living awareness of all this, who perceives himself as total gratuitousness and as absolute gift. He feels himself the “poor of God” inasmuch as he is aware that he has everything from God as pure gift and recognizes, accepts and joyfully lives this gift.

Introduction

Let us now consider the specific prayer of the Christian: the Our Father. It is the prayer that Jesus taught his disciples and that the whole Christian tradition has always felt as one of the most precious elements of the inheritance he left us.

1. Its Context and Structure

We know that in the Gospels we have two formulations of this prayer: that of Matt 6:9-13, which has become the one in common use in the universal Church, and the one offered to us by Luke 11:2-4. Let us read at once the Lukan version, which is the less well known:

“He said to them, ‘When you pray, say:
Father, hallowed be your name.
Your kingdom come.
Give us each day our daily bread.
And forgive us our sins,
for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us.
And do not bring us to the time of trial.’”

“In the first part, Luke lacks ‘Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven’, and in the second part the phrase ‘but deliver us from evil’ is missing.”

Now we must ask what was presumably the original version taught by Jesus. To this question, as it is formulated, no peremptory answer can be given, because each evangelist hands on the Our Father as it was used in his time in his own Church. There is, however, one thing to observe: the Our Father of Luke is entirely in St. Matthew; conversely, not all of Matthew’s version is present in Luke. One would therefore be led to conclude that it was Matthew who made additions. From what do we deduce this? From the supposition that Luke certainly did not shorten a prayer received as coming from Christ. In general one is led to make explicit and therefore to add, never to shorten. Moreover, in this case, we are dealing with a prayer that Jesus taught and that was held in the highest regard. We know that by apostolic tradition the Our Father could be said only by the baptized; even today in the Eucharist we have a venerable fragment, from which it appears that the Our Father could not be said lightly. We allude to the liturgical introduction: “At the Savior’s command and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say”. That is, there was an awareness that it was not a matter of saying words that Jesus had taught, but of praying with the very prayer of Jesus in an objective sense, that is, praying with the sentiments of Christ. In this mental context it is therefore difficult to say that Luke shortened it.

As regards the structure of the Our Father, it is very simple. We have a solemn introductory invocation: “Our Father, who art in heaven”, and then two parts: the first part contains three wishes addressed to God and concerning his Person: the hallowing of his name, the coming of his Kingdom, the fulfillment of his will. A hinge formula follows: “on earth as it is in heaven”, which links the first to the second part. The second part contains three petitions concerning man: the one concerning bread, the one concerning forgiveness, the petition for deliverance from evil. These are historical and concrete needs of man.

This structure of the Our Father gives us a first fundamental teaching. In the first part we ask God to bring about his Kingdom already begun by Jesus, we ask for a full revelation of his glory, that God manifest himself fully. It is a prayer that brings out the Christian in his true identity, as a man totally and radically oriented toward God and drawn in by the need for Him. The authentic Christian is a man whose soul is satisfied only by the bread that is God himself. The first teaching that derives from this is therefore the one concerning the true attitude of the one who prays. An attitude that is this gaze directed first of all to God, to his name, to his Kingdom, to his will, and only afterward to our needs; prayer made above all of humble adoration, giving priority to the realization of God’s loving plan for us according to the word of Jesus: “Strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt 6:33). One experiences the miracle of Providence only to the extent that one believes in it. Jesus, when he speaks to the disciples of their relationship with God, states: “For it is the Gentiles who strive for all these things; and indeed your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matt 6:32).

2. Analysis of the Contents

a) “Our Father, who art in heaven”

Here we have the first difference between the Matthean and the Lukan version. From the Gospels it results that when Jesus speaks personally with God he uses the appellative “Father” absolutely; when, on the other hand, he alludes to the relationship of the disciples with God he uses the expression “heavenly Father” or “your Father”. Now Luke shows that he knows this language of Jesus, which leads us to conclude that presumably Jesus in fact used the Jewish formula of Matthew. Luke perhaps, by saying only “Father”, already reflects the awareness of the early Church about the content of the appellative, which is new, is Christian, because already charged with the resonances of the message preached by Jesus about God the Father. In any case this discourse holds also, for the same reasons, for Matthew, in whom, therefore, the formula is Jewish, but the content is Christian. To invoke God in this way is equivalent to recognizing ourselves as children of God and consequently as brothers and sisters among ourselves. From this formulation emerges the awareness that, as Christians, one never prays alone, but always turns to God in communion with all who are children of God.

b) First Part: The Three Wishes

In the first part, in reality, rather than three petitions there is a single petition formulated in three different ways and with three different nuances. All three requests, in fact, contain a single object, which comes down to the definitive event of the Kingdom of God. This perspective is prompted by the fact that with the coming of Jesus we are now in the last times of the history of salvation. These three wishes, moreover, concern things that God alone must and can accomplish, they have as their effect tasks that exceed the mere capacities of man. With these petitions the one who prays asks God that He be the one to accomplish what is requested. And it is the very formulation of the text that pushes us toward this meaning with the presence of verbs in the passive voice; this is the so-called “theological passive”, used to indicate God as subject while avoiding naming his name. In the time of Jesus, in fact, in the Jewish world the name of God was unnameable, ineffable, and therefore when one had to speak of God acting, presenting him as subject, one used the verb in the passive or, as an expedient, other words (“kingdom of heaven” in place of “kingdom of God”).

– “Hallowed be your name”

The name, in the Semitic world, says the entitative, objective value of the person, says what the person is in himself. Consequently, to pronounce the name of a person means to have power over the person himself, to possess him; if one can pronounce his name it means that one can possess the person who is identified with the name. In this mental context “to hallow the name of God” means to recognize that God is totally different from us, that He is the wholly other, that He is the Absolute, the Transcendent, the Infinite.

– “Your kingdom come”

The Kingdom of God preached by Jesus is that existential situation in which between God and man a full communion is realized, in which He has free space in our life, can reign in it freely and fully. This full fusion of love between God and man constitutes the Kingdom of God preached by Jesus in the Gospels. With this petition we ask that this Kingdom of God come, we ask for its glorious revelation through its coming, which will put an end to the waiting of the faithful for the fulfillment of all things. Our historical world, today as tomorrow, is a world of opposition to God, so that the forces of evil seem to have the upper hand. The further one goes on in life, the more one finds oneself far from the shore of what God wants us to be and of what we ourselves would like to be. One is aware that God is that boundless sea, in which the more one sails the more one sees its boundless breadth and the farther one feels from the harbor. With this petition, therefore, one asks not only for the definitive revelation of God’s sovereignty, but one asks also for the definitive destruction of the forces of evil. One prays that God put an end to the present time and definitively establish the world to come.

– “Your will be done”

In the petition there is also an implicit prayer: “Grant, O Lord, that we may do your will so as not to hinder you from doing yours”. God does not do violence to us, but offers himself, proposes himself. Here we ask God to carry out his will, to do himself what he has decided for us, and at the same time we also ask that we human beings may know how to respect and welcome this his will of salvation, that we may be capable of accepting his gift. With this we implicitly ask that God fulfill the promise of renewing our heart with his Spirit.

– “On earth as it is in heaven”

For the ancients heaven was by definition the place of the Divinity, because heaven was impassable to man. With this expression we ask God that what already exists in heaven be realized on earth. Earth is the place in which the forces of evil exercise their influence and fight against God and against his faithful. We ask, therefore, that our history, our habitat, our humanity become what it ought to be, that for which God created it.

c) Second Part: The Three Petitions

After the three preceding wishes, centered essentially on God, the believer now turns to his own real needs and presents them to the Lord with immense trust.

– “Give us this day our daily bread”

The petition is present in Luke too, but its formulation, as we already know, is different from Matthew’s: “Give us each day our daily bread”. In Matthew there is a punctual, well-circumscribed imperative: “give us today”; the orientation in the Matthean petition is therefore toward the bread we need today. In Luke, on the other hand, we again have an imperative, but in the present tense, which in the Greek language evokes the perspective of continuity. The question arises what kind of bread is meant here. Certainly we ask the Lord for what is necessary for daily life, but in the believer’s perspective the horizons are much broader and do not exclude the request for what is necessary for true life, the full and imperishable life, which Jesus has promised us, merited and given. At times it might be the difficulty of adhering to God, of accepting his will; at other times it might be the difficulty of overcoming a trial; that is, everything that constitutes the need for a true communion with God enters into this petition.

The spirit of this petition is enclosed in the verbal tense of the formulation. In Matthew’s text there is an underlining of the sense of full abandonment to Providence, of total trust; the soul of the child surfaces in it, who does not ask for tomorrow, but for the immediate moment. It is a petition that reflects the stature of the one who prays, the breadth and depth of his soul.

– “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors”

The petition is present in Luke too, though in a different way: “Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us”. Matthew has the term “debts”; Luke speaks instead of “sins”. Matthew’s use of “debts” reflects biblical language. In the Bible “debt”, in a religious perspective, says the situation of man before God. Man before God is always the insolvent debtor, above all because he is a sinner, because he is not capable of fidelity to Him, who, on the contrary, is immensely faithful and generous. Moreover, man owes everything to God, his is an existential debt toward the Lord, inasmuch as he has received from Him all that he is. In this perspective the “forgive us our debts” concerns “sin” in its broadest sense.

But at the same time we also set a clause: “Forgive our unfaithfulness as we forgive our debtors”. It is the condition that we set, asking God to forgive us. It follows, then, that whoever forgives much will be forgiven much. We should recall in Matt 5:23-24 the invitation not to delay reconciliation even at the cost of interrupting worship: “So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift”. In the same line it is well to recall the message of Matt 18:21-35 on the duty and breadth of forgiveness. In the Our Father we do not ask God to conform his will to ours, because here the “as we forgive” does not express a relationship of equality and reciprocity between human forgiveness and divine forgiveness. Rather we must forgive, so that our petition may not be hypocritical. It is not God’s forgiveness that is conditioned by ours, but it is the value of our petition that is conditioned by our prior forgiveness.

– “Do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one”

The petition is composed of two parts, a positive and a negative one. Temptation here is anything that solicits us to sin. In the Greek text, however, the term used indicates something more, it connotes both trial in the general sense and temptation in the technical sense. Even when we commit sin we are always under God’s hold; we sin using all those energies that God is giving us at the very moment in which we go against Him. In the more recent biblical texts it is said that God tests, and no longer that God makes one sin in order to see man’s fidelity, as we read in the more ancient texts. God tests Abraham, tests the Prophets, tests the people in the desert in order to bring out the sincerity of their religious soul. Then “do not bring us to the time of trial” means that we ask God to avoid a trial such that there is a risk of not being able to overcome it. It is useful to recall what St. Paul says to the Corinthians: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor 10:13). In our case we do not ask the Lord to take us out of temptation, but not to permit trials beyond our strength. Every man is tempted, every man has trials; the object of the petition is therefore to be protected in temptation, to be helped to overcome it. It is the meaning we find in Matt 26:41, in Jesus’ admonition in Gethsemane: “Stay awake and pray that you may not come into the time of trial”, that is, so as not to succumb in temptation. Jesus says this to the Twelve precisely with regard to his approaching Passion, which will be for the Twelve a great temptation, a decisive trial for their faith, an inevitable examination which they will have to pass.

In this perspective we do not ask here to be protected from the normal daily temptations, but to be protected from that trial which is capable of provoking in us apostasy, a trial whose object is God. It is, obviously, a question of apostasy in a broad sense, of that attitude of soul which seeks, as far as possible, to do without God, of that politely ignoring him, of that setting up fences so that He may not come too close to us and may not take too much; in short, of the unconfessed wish that God be a little less free in our regard, leaving us a vital space of our own.

We understand, then, the petition: “rescue us from the evil one”, which perhaps should be understood in the sense of “deliver us from the Evil One”. In fact Jesus came essentially to engage in the struggle against the Evil One, and this purpose is underlined by all his exorcistic activity as we have it in the Synoptics, as well as by Jesus’ initial temptation in the desert. This fact, I believe, sheds light on the meaning to be given here to the term in the sense of “Evil One”. It is, that is, a question of that reality of evil which is too great to be merely an episodic situation of evil. We are in the line of John 17:15: “I am not asking you to take them out of the world, but I ask you to protect them from the evil one”. Jesus, in his priestly prayer, prayed this petition of the Our Father for us.

This last datum too lets us see the broad horizons of the Our Father. Each of its petitions, in fact, exudes universalistic horizons and reveals unsuspected abysmal depths. This is why this prayer was immediately perceived as the prayer par excellence, indeed not only as the most beautiful prayer of the Christian, but as the one that defines him. Only the authentic Christian can pray it in truth, and in fact in antiquity its recitation was permitted only to the baptized. We are thus brought back to the beginning of our long historical journey through the prayer of the “poor of God”. These perspectives of the Our Father, in fact, precisely in their sense of trust, of abandonment, of seeking God, of tension toward Him, lead us back once again to the great horizons and the great dimensions of the prayer of the “poor of God” of the OT.
